citations.quote:
Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. For every $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and every multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$,
$$\mathcal F(D^\alpha u)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal Fu\qquad\text{in }\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n),$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the distributional derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] and $\mathcal F$ is
the negative-sign $2\pi$-normalized transform. Moreover, if $u=u_f$ and
$D^\alpha u=u_g$ for $L^2$ classes $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ and their regular
distributions, then the unitary Plancherel transforms satisfy
$$\mathcal F_2g(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal F_2f(\xi)\qquad\text{for almost every }\xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
The second assertion compares the Plancherel classes only; it neither asserts
pointwise values of arbitrary representatives nor presupposes any Sobolev-space
notation.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and use complex
scalars. Write $W^{k,2}=W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for the weak-derivative
Sobolev space of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], whose classes carry
the weak derivatives $D^\alpha f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for
$|\alpha|\le k$ and the norm
$$\|f\|_{W^{k,2}}=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha f\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$
and let $H^k=H^k(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion
of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical
embedding $E_k:H^k\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Let
$u_f\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ denote the regular tempered distribution of
an $L^2$ class $f$. Then:

1. $E_k[H^k]=\{u_f:f\in W^{k,2}\}$, and
   $\Phi(f):=E_k^{-1}(u_f)$ is a bijection
   $\Phi:W^{k,2}\to H^k$. Thus, under the regular-distribution embedding,
   $W^{k,2}$ and $H^k$ are the same subspace of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.
2. There are constants $0<c_k\le C_k<\infty$, depending only on $n$ and $k$,
   with
$$c_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2\le\|f\|_{W^{k,2}} \le C_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2,$$
   and $\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2=\|\Phi(f)\|_{H^k}$. Hence the
   weak-derivative norm and the bracket-weighted $L^2$ norm are equivalent,
   and the latter is also equivalent to
   $\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}\mathcal F_2f\|_2$, by
$$\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2\le\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}h\|_2 \le(2\pi)^k\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2,\qquad h\in L^2 .$$
3. The three norm expressions are **not** identical in general: the
   bracket-weighted norm differs from both the weak-derivative norm and the
   Laplacian-weighted norm, as the Gaussian computation in the proof shows.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Work on a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first variable. Let $A$ be self-adjoint and let $B$ be symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and
$A$-bound less than one ([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]]).
Then $A+B$ with domain $D(A)$ is self-adjoint. If $A$ is merely essentially
self-adjoint and $B$ is symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and $A$-bound less
than one, then $A+B$ on $D(A)$ is essentially self-adjoint and its closure is
the self-adjoint operator obtained by applying the first part to $\overline A$
and the graph-norm extension of $B|_{D(A)}$ to $D(\overline A)$. If $A\ge\gamma$ and
$(a,b)$ is an admissible pair for $B$ with $a<1$, then
$A+B\ge\gamma-\max\{a|\gamma|+b,\ b/(1-a)\}$.

Let $A$ be a linear operator on $H$ with domain $D(A)$. An operator $B$ is
**$A$-bounded**, or **relatively bounded with respect to $A$**, when
$D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and there are finite constants $a,b\ge0$ with
$$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|\qquad\text{for all }x\in D(A).$$
The infimum of the admissible constants $a$ is the **$A$-bound** of $B$, and
one says the $A$-bound is *below one* when some $a<1$ is admissible.

**Equivalent form.** $B$ is $A$-bounded exactly when $B$ is bounded on $D(A)$
for the graph norm $\|x\|_A=(\|x\|^2+\|Ax\|^2)^{1/2}$ of
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]: each estimate
$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|$ gives
$\|Bx\|\le\max(a,b)\sqrt2\,\|x\|_A$, and conversely a graph-norm bound
$\|Bx\|\le C\|x\|_A$ gives the estimate with $a=b=C$. The constant $b$ is not
intrinsic, and no closedness, density or resolvent hypothesis is needed for
the definition. If $A$ is closed with nonempty resolvent set, then $A$-bounded
operators are exactly those with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ for which $BR_A(z)$ is
bounded for some, equivalently every, $z\in\rho(A)$
([[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]]). Indeed, an
$A$-bound makes $BR_A(z)$ bounded because
$AR_A(z)=zR_A(z)-I$; conversely, if $BR_A(z)$ is bounded, then
$Bx=BR_A(z)(z-A)x$ gives an $A$-bound. Thus boundedness for one resolvent
implies relative boundedness and hence boundedness for every resolvent. This
is used in the Kato-Rellich theorem below and recorded here as an interface.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with
spectral projection valued measure $E$, and set
$U(t):=e^{itT}=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{it\lambda}\,dE(\lambda)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$.
Then $U$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group,
$U(t)D(T)=D(T)$ and $TU(t)=U(t)T$ on $D(T)$, and the derivative
$\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(U(t)x-x)$ exists exactly for $x\in D(T)$, where it equals
$iTx$. Thus the generator of $U$ is $G=iT$, with $D(G)=D(T)$.

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

derivations.claim: [Density and symmetry of the multiplier] By [F8], the defined $L^2$ space $H$ is a complex Hilbert space. For $f\in H$ and $n\ge1$ put $f_n:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|a|\le n\}}$. Then $af_n$ is bounded by $n|f_n|$, so $f_n\in D(M_a)$, and $f_n\to f$ in $H$ by [F1] applied to $|f_n-f|^2\le|f|^2$; hence $D(M_a)$ is dense. For $f,g\in D(M_a)$ the integral $\int af\overline g$ is defined and equals $\int f\overline{ag}$ because $a$ is real-valued, so $\langle M_af,g\rangle=\langle f,M_ag\rangle$: $M_a$ is symmetric.

[Adjoint domain of the multiplier] Let $g\in D(M_a^*)$ with representing vector $h=M_a^*g$, so $\int af\overline g=\int f\overline h$ for all $f\in D(M_a)$. Fix $n$ and restrict to $f\in H$ vanishing off $E_n:=\{|a|\le n\}$; every such $f$ lies in $D(M_a)$, and the identity reads $\int_{E_n}(a\overline g-\overline h)f=0$ for all $f\in L^2(E_n)$, so $h=ag$ a.e. on $E_n$; as $E_n\uparrow\mathbb R^d$, $h=ag$ a.e., and since $h\in H$, $ag\in H$ and $g\in D(M_a)$. Conversely every $g\in D(M_a)$ satisfies the adjoint identity with $h=M_ag$. Hence $D(M_a^*)=D(M_a)$ and $M_a^*=M_a$: $M_a$ is self-adjoint, giving (a).

[Unitary conjugation] Let $T:=M_{c|\xi|^2+b}$, self-adjoint on $D(T)=\{g:c|\xi|^2g\in H\}$ by step 2.1 applied to the real finite-valued function $c|\xi|^2+b$. Define $H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*T\mathcal F_2$ on $D(H_0)=\mathcal F_2^{-1}D(T)=\{f:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}$. For $x,y\in D(H_0)$, $\langle H_0x,y\rangle=\langle T\mathcal F_2x,\mathcal F_2y\rangle$ by unitarity of $\mathcal F_2$ [F3]. If $y\in D(H_0^*)$, the functional $x\mapsto\langle H_0x,y\rangle$ is bounded on $D(H_0)$; conjugating by the unitary $\mathcal F_2$ shows that $g\mapsto\langle Tg,\mathcal F_2y\rangle$ is bounded on $D(T)$, so $\mathcal F_2y\in D(T^*)=D(T)$ and hence $y\in D(H_0)$ with $H_0^*y=\mathcal F_2^*T^*\mathcal F_2y=H_0y$; the reverse inclusion is immediate from the symmetry identity. Thus $H_0$ is self-adjoint.

[Domain, lower bound and free action] By [F5], $D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d)$ as a set with equivalent norms. For $f\in D(H_0)$ the pairing with $f$ is computed in the $\xi$-variable, where multiplication by $c|\xi|^2+b\ge b$ gives $\langle H_0f,f\rangle=\int(c|\xi|^2+b)|\mathcal F_2f(\xi)|^2d\xi\ge b\|\mathcal F_2f\|^2=b\|f\|^2$, so $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense. For a Schwartz function $f$, [F4] gives $\mathcal F_2(-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf)(\xi)=(c|\xi|^2+b)\mathcal F_2f(\xi)$ a.e.; both sides are continuous representatives, and Plancherel inversion identifies them as elements of $H$, so $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$. This is (b).

[Bounded perturbation by Kato-Rellich] Let $V$ be real with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and let $M_V$ be the bounded multiplication operator on $H$. Then $D(H_0)\subseteq D(M_V)=H$, $M_V$ is symmetric because $V$ is real, and $\|M_Vf\|\le\|V\|_\infty\|f\|$ for every $f\in D(H_0)$, so the $H_0$-bound of $M_V$ is $0<1$ with admissible pair $(0,\|V\|_\infty)$ ([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]]). By [F6] the operator $H=H_0+M_V$ on $D(H_0)$ is self-adjoint and, since $H_0\ge b$, satisfies $H\ge b-\max\{0\cdot|b|+\|V\|_\infty,\ \|V\|_\infty\}=b-\|V\|_\infty$, hence is bounded below.

[Unitary dynamics] Applying [F7] to the self-adjoint $H$ of step 5.1 yields that $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group, $e^{itH}D(H)=D(H)$, and the difference quotients converge exactly on $D(H)$; the physical convention $t\mapsto e^{-itH}$ is the same group at negative time. No claim in this item extends to unbounded or singular $V$, which are excluded by the boundedness and measurability hypotheses recorded in [F6].

citations.quote:
Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

A finite family of finite-valued random variables $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **mutually independent** when for every nonempty $J\subseteq I$ and every selection $x_j\in X_j(\Omega)$,
$$\mathbb P(X_j=x_j\text{ for every }j\in J)=\prod_{j\in J}\mathbb P(X_j=x_j).$$
It is **pairwise independent** when this identity is required only for two distinct indices. The empty family is mutually independent vacuously, and a one-member family is mutually independent.

For $p\in[0,1]$, a **Bernoulli$(p)$ random variable** takes the value $1$ with probability $p$ and $0$ with probability $1-p$.

For $n\in\mathbb N$, a **binomial$(n,p)$ random variable** is a sum $X=\sum_{i<n}X_i$ of $n$ mutually independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables. When $n=0$, this is the constant zero random variable.

If $X$ is Bernoulli$(p)$, then $\mathbb E[X]=p$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=p(1-p)$. If $S$ is binomial$(n,p)$, then
$$\mathbb E[S]=np,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(S)=np(1-p).$$
These formulas include $p=0$, $p=1$, and $n=0$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

If $X$ is a square-integrable real random variable and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge a)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.$$

Let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Write

$$\mathcal{W}(n,m) := \Big\{\, k : m \to \mathbb{N} \ \Big|\ \sum_{i<m} k_i = n \,\Big\},$$

the set of $m$-tuples of naturals summing to $n$, the sum being the
$\mathbb{N}$-valued one of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]].

**$\mathcal{W}(n,m)$ is finite.** If $\sum_{i<m}k_i = n$ then each $k_i \le n$ by
the monotonicity clause of
[[lem-nat-finite-sum-laws-and-the-canonical-embedding]] (a term of a sum of
naturals is at most the sum), so $\mathcal{W}(n,m)$ is a subset of the set of
functions $m \to \sigma(n)$, which is finite by
[[thm-cardinality-of-a-set-of-functions]]; now apply
[[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]].

**Block decompositions as colourings.** For a finite set $A$ and $k : m \to
\mathbb{N}$ put

$$\mathcal{B}(A,k) := \big\{\, c : A \to m \ \big|\ \lvert c^{-1}[\{i\}]\rvert = k_i \text{ for every } i < m \,\big\}.$$

A colouring $c$ is the same thing as an ordered decomposition of $A$ into the $m$
blocks $c^{-1}[\{0\}], \dots, c^{-1}[\{m-1\}]$; presenting it as a function makes
the blocks a partition of $A$ automatically, so that
[[thm-sum-rule]] and [[thm-cardinality-of-a-set-of-functions]] apply verbatim.
$\mathcal{B}(A,k)$ is a subset of the finite set $m^{A}$, hence finite.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=1cm,y=0.72cm]
  \draw (0,1.75) ellipse (0.9 and 2.25);
  \draw (4.4,1.75) ellipse (0.9 and 1.65);
  \node at (0,4.35) {$A$};
  \node at (4.4,3.8) {$m=3$};
  \node (a1) at (0,3.25) {$a_1$};
  \node (a2) at (0,2.65) {$a_2$};
  \node (b1) at (0,1.75) {$b_1$};
  \node (c1) at (0,0.85) {$c_1$};
  \node (c2) at (0,0.25) {$c_2$};
  \node (c3) at (0,-0.35) {$c_3$};
  \node (z0) at (4.4,2.75) {$0$};
  \node (z1) at (4.4,1.75) {$1$};
  \node (z2) at (4.4,0.75) {$2$};
  \draw[->] (a1) -- (z0);
  \draw[->] (a2) -- (z0);
  \draw[->] (b1) -- (z1);
  \draw[->] (c1) -- (z2);
  \draw[->] (c2) -- (z2);
  \draw[->] (c3) -- (z2);
  \node at (2.2,-1.05) {$(|c^{-1}(0)|,|c^{-1}(1)|,|c^{-1}(2)|)=(2,1,3)$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

**The hypothesis is part of the definition, and it is forced.** The fibres
$c^{-1}[\{i\}]$, $i < m$, are pairwise disjoint with union $A$, so
[[thm-sum-rule]] gives
$\lvert A\rvert = \sum_{i<m}\lvert c^{-1}[\{i\}]\rvert = \sum_{i<m}k_i$ for any
$c \in \mathcal{B}(A,k)$. Hence $\mathcal{B}(A,k) = \varnothing$ unless
$k \in \mathcal{W}(\lvert A\rvert, m)$, and the coefficient is defined only under
that hypothesis.

**$\lvert\mathcal{B}(A,k)\rvert$ depends only on $\lvert A\rvert$.** If
$h : A \to A'$ is a bijection then $c \mapsto c \circ h^{-1}$ maps
$\mathcal{B}(A,k)$ to $\mathcal{B}(A',k)$, because
$(c\circ h^{-1})^{-1}[\{i\}] = h\big[c^{-1}[\{i\}]\big]$ has the same cardinality
as $c^{-1}[\{i\}]$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]); and $c' \mapsto c' \circ h$ is
its two-sided inverse.

**Definition.** For $k \in \mathcal{W}(n,m)$ set

$$\binom{n}{k_0,\dots,k_{m-1}} := \big\lvert\mathcal{B}(n,k)\big\rvert \in \mathbb{N},$$

abbreviated $\binom{n}{k}$ when the tuple is named. By the previous paragraph,
$\lvert\mathcal{B}(A,k)\rvert = \binom{\lvert A\rvert}{k}$ for every finite $A$
with $\lvert A\rvert = n$. Like the binomial coefficient, it is **defined as a
count**, so it is a natural number by construction.

**Boundary cases.**

- $m = 0$. The empty sum is $0$, so $\mathcal{W}(n,0)$ is nonempty only for
  $n = 0$, where its single element is the empty tuple. And
  $\mathcal{B}(\varnothing, ())$ contains exactly the empty function, so
  $\binom{0}{\ } = 1$.
- A block of size $0$ is allowed: $k_i = 0$ simply means
  $c^{-1}[\{i\}] = \varnothing$.
- $m = 2$ recovers the binomial coefficient: for $k \le n$,
  $\binom{n}{k,\,n-k} = \binom{n}{k}$. The map $c \mapsto c^{-1}[\{0\}]$ sends
  $\mathcal{B}(A,(k,n-k))$ into $[A]^{k}$, and $S \mapsto$ the colouring taking
  the value $0$ on $S$ and $1$ off it is its two-sided inverse, the second fibre
  having cardinality $n - k$ by [[thm-sum-rule]]. So the two notations do not
  collide.

derivations.claim: [Pointwise CHSH identity] Fix $\omega\in\Omega$. Since $B_0(\omega),B_1(\omega)\in\{-1,1\}$, the numbers $B_0(\omega)+B_1(\omega)$ and $B_0(\omega)-B_1(\omega)$ are $\pm2$ or $0$, and exactly one of them is nonzero: the first is $0$ precisely when $B_1(\omega)=-B_0(\omega)$, in which case the second is $\pm2$, and otherwise the first is $\pm2$ and the second $0$. Hence $A_0(B_0+B_1)+A_1(B_0-B_1)$ equals $\pm2$ at every $\omega$, so its absolute value is bounded by $2$ pointwise and $\mathbb E[A_0B_0]+\mathbb E[A_0B_1]+\mathbb E[A_1B_0]-\mathbb E[A_1B_1]=\mathbb E[A_0(B_0+B_1)+A_1(B_0-B_1)]$ by linearity [F2], the variables being bounded hence integrable. The monotonicity and modulus bound of [F2] applied to the pointwise bound $-2\le A_0(B_0+B_1)+A_1(B_0-B_1)\le2$ give the stated $\le2$ bound.

[Positive-probability sequences] By mutual independence [F3] applied to the full index set $J=\{1,\dots,N\}$ and the selection $x_k=j_k$, $\mathbb P(X_k=j_k\text{ for all }k)=\prod_k\mathbb P(X_k=j_k)=\prod_kp_{j_k}$, which is a product of positive reals and hence positive. If an event $R$ is disjoint from $\{X_k=j_k\text{ for all }k\}$, then $\mathbb P(R)\le1-\prod_kp_{j_k}<1$ by additivity and complementation [F1].

[Binomial frequency moments] By [F4], $S$ is a sum of $N$ mutually independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables, with $\mathbb E[S]=Np$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S)=Np(1-p)$. Linearity [F2] gives $\mathbb E[S/N]=\frac1N\mathbb E[S]=p$; and by the definition of variance [F5], $\operatorname{Var}(S/N)=\mathbb E[(S/N-p)^2]=\frac1{N^2}\mathbb E[(S-Np)^2]=\frac1{N^2}\operatorname{Var}(S)=\frac{p(1-p)}N$. Applying the Chebyshev inequality [F5] to the square-integrable variable $S/N$ with parameter $\varepsilon>0$ gives $\mathbb P(|S/N-p|\ge\varepsilon)\le p(1-p)/(N\varepsilon^2)$.

[Multinomial count law] A sequence $(j_1,\dots,j_N)$ is exactly a function $c:\{1,\dots,N\}\to\{1,\dots,m\}$, with fibre sizes $n_j$; by [F6] the number of such functions with prescribed fibre sizes is $\binom{N}{n_1,\dots,n_m}$. By independence [F3] each of these sequences has probability $\prod_kp_{j_k}=\prod_jp_j^{n_j}$, because the exponent of $p_j$ is the number of $k$ with $j_k=j$, namely $n_j$; when $n_j=0$ the sequence contains no factor $p_j$, and the displayed product convention in (d) assigns that factor the value $1$, also when $p_j=0$. The count event is the disjoint union of the corresponding singletons, so finite additivity [F1] gives probability $\binom{N}{n_1,\dots,n_m}\prod_jp_j^{n_j}$.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

Let $\mathcal B=(b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1})$ be an ordered basis of $V$. The unique
coordinates $v=\sum_{j<n}x_jb_j$ form the **coordinate column**
$[v]_{\mathcal B}\in M_{n\times1}(F)$, whose $j$-th entry is $x_j$.

Let $\mathcal C=(c_0,\ldots,c_{m-1})$ be an ordered basis of $W$ and let
$T:V\to W$ be linear. The **matrix of $T$ relative to $\mathcal B$ and
$\mathcal C$** is the matrix
$[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ whose $j$-th column is
$[T(b_j)]_{\mathcal C}$. Equivalently, if
$T(b_j)=\sum_{i<m}t_{ij}c_i$, then
$([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C})_{ij}=t_{ij}$.

For an empty ordered basis, these definitions give the unique coordinate column
or matrix of the corresponding zero-sized shape.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be normal. If $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r$ are the distinct eigenvalues of $T$,
then there are pairwise orthogonal projections $P_1,\dots,P_r$ such that

$$T=\sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j P_j,$$

each $P_j$ projects onto the eigenspace $E_{\lambda_j}(T)$, and every $P_j$ is
a polynomial in $T$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

derivations.claim: [Existence and uniqueness of the partial trace] Define $\operatorname{Tr}_WR:=\sum_{j=1}^n\varphi_jR\iota_j$, a linear endomorphism of $V$. Computed in the basis $(e_i\otimes f_j)$ and using [F2], the matrix of $\varphi_j$ contracts the $W$-index into $f_j$, and the total matrix of $\operatorname{Tr}_WR$ has entries $(\operatorname{Tr}_WR)_{i i'}=\sum_jR_{ij,i'j}$; hence, with $(A)_{i'i''}$ the matrix of $A$, $\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{Tr}_WR)A)=\sum_{i,i',j}R_{ij,i'j}A_{i'i}=\operatorname{tr}(R(A\otimes I_W))$. Uniqueness: if $S$ and $S'$ both satisfy the pairing identity, then $\operatorname{tr}((S-S')A)=0$ for all $A$; taking $A=T_{\alpha,\beta}$ (the rank-one endomorphism $v\mapsto\langle v,\beta\rangle\alpha$) for $\alpha,\beta$ ranging over a basis of $V$ and using [F1] and [F2] extracts every matrix entry of $S-S'$, so $S=S'$. Basis independence: the defining identity involves only the basis-independent trace [F2]; equivalently the formula with another orthonormal basis $(g_j)$ yields the same operator by the uniqueness just proved.

[Positivity and trace preservation] If $R\ge0$ then for every $x\in V$, $\langle(\operatorname{Tr}_WR)x,x\rangle=\sum_j\langle R(x\otimes f_j),x\otimes f_j\rangle\ge0$ because $R\ge0$ [F4] and each summand is a nonnegative real; hence $\operatorname{Tr}_WR\ge0$. Taking $A=I_V$ in the defining identity gives $\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Tr}_WR=\operatorname{tr}R$; consequently a density matrix $R$ (positive, $\operatorname{tr}R=1$, in the sense of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]) has $\operatorname{Tr}_WR\ge0$ and trace $1$, so $(\operatorname{Tr}_W)$ maps density matrices to density matrices.

[Reduced state of a pure vector] Let $\Psi=\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}e_i\otimes f_j$ and define $C:W\to V$ by $Cf_j=\sum_ic_{ij}e_i$, so that $\Psi=\sum_jCf_j\otimes f_j$ by [F1] (insert the expansions of the $Cf_j$). For the rank-one endomorphism $T_{\Psi,\Psi}$ and $A\in\operatorname{End}(V)$, the defining identity of step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{Tr}_WT_{\Psi,\Psi})A)=\operatorname{tr}(T_{\Psi,\Psi}(A\otimes I))=\langle(A\otimes I)\Psi,\Psi\rangle$, and substituting the expansion yields $\sum_{i,i'}\langle A e_i,e_{i'}\rangle\sum_jc_{ij}\overline{c_{i'j}}=\operatorname{tr}(A\,CC^*)$, using the matrix of $CC^*$ in the basis $(e_i)$. Since this holds for all $A$ and the operator is determined by its pairings with all $A$ (step 1.1), $\operatorname{Tr}_WT_{\Psi,\Psi}=CC^*$.

[Schmidt expansion with the complex convention] Apply [F3] to the coefficient map $C$: there are orthonormal right singular vectors $q_r\in W$ and left singular vectors $v_r\in V$ such that $Cf_j=\sum_rs_r\langle f_j,q_r\rangle v_r$. Define $u_r:=\sum_j\langle f_j,q_r\rangle f_j$, the coordinate conjugate of $q_r$ in the fixed basis $(f_j)$. The coordinate conjugation reverses inner products, so $\langle u_r,u_t\rangle=\overline{\langle q_r,q_t\rangle}=\delta_{rt}$. Substituting the formula for $Cf_j$ into $\Psi=\sum_jCf_j\otimes f_j$ gives $\Psi=\sum_rs_rv_r\otimes u_r$. Thus the claimed Schmidt expansion holds, with singular values $s_r$ of $C$. Changing the factor bases changes the coefficient matrix by unitary matrices (with transpose rather than adjoint on the second factor); hence the singular values remain unchanged. Orthogonality of the elementary Schmidt products gives $\|\Psi\|^2=\sum_rs_r^2$.

[Purity and the product criterion] By steps 2.2 and 3.1, $\rho=\operatorname{Tr}_WT_{\Psi,\Psi}=CC^*$ has eigenvalues $s_r^2$ with multiplicity by [F3], so for $\|\Psi\|=1$ we have $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2=\sum_rs_r^4$ and $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1=\sum_rs_r^2$. Since all $s_r$ are positive, $\sum_rs_r^4\le(\sum_rs_r^2)^2=1$ with equality exactly when at most one $s_r$ is nonzero, i.e. $k=1$; and $k=1$ means $\Psi=s_1v_1\otimes u_1$ is a product vector, conversely a product vector has $C$ of rank one by step 2.2. This is the stated criterion; it concerns pure vectors only.

[Finite nonselective no-signalling] Let $(M_a)$ satisfy $\sum_aM_a^*M_a=I_W$. For $A\in\operatorname{End}(V)$, using the defining identity of step 1.1 and the identity $(I\otimes M_a^*)(A\otimes I)=(A\otimes M_a^*)$ together with cyclicity [F2] inside the finite trace, $\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_W\sum_a(I\otimes M_a)R(I\otimes M_a^*))A\bigr)=\sum_a\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R(A\otimes M_a^*M_a)\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R(A\otimes\sum_aM_a^*M_a)\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R(A\otimes I)\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_WR)A\bigr)$; since this holds for every $A$, the uniqueness in step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{Tr}_W(\sum_a(I\otimes M_a)R(I\otimes M_a^*))=\operatorname{Tr}_WR$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Here $|A|^{1/2}$ denotes the unbounded PVM integral $f(E_A)$ for $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{1/2}$, with domain $D(f(E_A))=\{\psi:\int |\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty\}$ as in [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

derivations.claim: [POVM probabilities] By [F4], $\rho=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ with $(u_n)$ orthonormal and $\sum_nw_n=1$. Then $p_a=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)=\sum_nw_n\langle F_au_n,u_n\rangle$ by linearity of the finite trace [F3], and each term is non-negative because $F_a\ge0$ [F2]; hence $p_a\ge0$. Summing over $a$ and using linearity, $\sum_ap_a=\sum_nw_n\langle(\sum_aF_a)u_n,u_n\rangle=\sum_nw_n=1$.

[Lüders instance] For $M_0=P$ and $M_1=I-P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ [F5], $M_0^*M_0=P^2=P$ and $M_1^*M_1=(I-P)^2=I-P$, so $\sum_jM_j^*M_j=I$ and the effects are $F_0=P$, $F_1=I-P$; the updates are $I_0(\rho)=P\rho P$, $I_1(\rho)=(I-P)\rho(I-P)$.

[Update traces and positivity] Let $F_a=\sum_rM_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}$. Then $\operatorname{tr}I_a(\rho)=\sum_r\operatorname{tr}(M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*)=\sum_r\operatorname{tr}(\rho M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)=p_a$, by cyclicity [F3]. For each $r$, $(M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*)^*=M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*$ because $\rho=\rho^*$; hence $I_a(\rho)$ is self-adjoint. For $x\in H$, $\langle I_a(\rho)x,x\rangle=\sum_r\langle M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^*x,x\rangle=\sum_r\langle\rho (M_{a,r}^*x),M_{a,r}^*x\rangle\ge0$ because $\rho\ge0$; thus $I_a(\rho)\ge0$. If $p_a>0$, then $I_a(\rho)/p_a$ has trace $1$ and is positive, hence is a density operator in the sense of [F4]. The effects of a normalized instrument form a POVM: each $M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}$ is non-negative, and both $F_a$ and $I-F_a=\sum_{(b,r):b\ne a}M_{b,r}^*M_{b,r}$ are non-negative, so $0\le F_a\le I$. This is (b).

[Two instruments with equal effects] On $H=\mathbb C^2$ with orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2)$ let $F_0=T_{e_1,e_1}$, $F_1=T_{e_2,e_2}$ and let $\sigma$ be the swap $\sigma e_1=e_2$, $\sigma e_2=e_1$, so that $\sigma^*\sigma=I$ by [F5]. Instrument A: $M_{0,1}:=F_0$, $M_{1,1}:=F_1$. Instrument B: $M_{0,1}:=\sigma F_0$, $M_{1,1}:=F_1$. Both are normalized: $F_0^*F_0+F_1^*F_1=F_0+F_1=I$, and $(\sigma F_0)^*(\sigma F_0)=F_0\sigma^*\sigma F_0=F_0^2=F_0$, so $F_1+F_0=I$. Their effect families coincide, but their updates differ on $\rho=\tfrac12I$: $I_0^A(\rho)=\tfrac12F_0=\tfrac12\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ while $I_0^B(\rho)=\tfrac12\sigma F_0\sigma=\tfrac12\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$, by $\sigma T_{e_1,e_1}\sigma=T_{\sigma e_1,\sigma e_1}=T_{e_2,e_2}$. This is (d).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,H',K,K'$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let $S\in\mathcal B(H,H')$, $T\in\mathcal B(K,K')$ be bounded linear operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Write $H\widehat\otimes K$ for the completion of the algebraic tensor product constructed in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], with inclusion $\kappa$.

(a) There is a unique bounded linear operator $S\otimes T: H\widehat\otimes K\to H'\widehat\otimes K'$ with $(S\otimes T)\kappa(u\otimes v)=\kappa'(Su\otimes Tv)$ for all $u\in H$, $v\in K$, and it satisfies $\|S\otimes T\|\le\|S\|\,\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]).

(b) For Hilbert spaces $H'',K''$ and bounded $S':H''\to H$, $T':K''\to K$, one has $(S\otimes T)(S'\otimes T')=(SS')\otimes(TT')$. In particular, for endomorphisms $S:H\to H$, $T:K\to K$, the endomorphisms $S\otimes I_K$ and $I_H\otimes T$ commute and their composite is $S\otimes T$.

(c) The Hilbert adjoint ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]) is $(S\otimes T)^*=S^*\otimes T^*$.

(d) If $S,T$ are unitary, then so is $S\otimes T$. No extension of unbounded maps, and no algebraic manipulation of domains of unbounded operators, is asserted.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ be a finite list of $R$-modules. Any parenthesized tensor product

$$T=M_1\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RM_k$$

represents $R$-multilinear maps from $M_1\times\cdots\times M_k$: for every $R$-module $P$, composition with $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\mapsto m_1\otimes\cdots\otimes m_k$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Hom}_R(T,P)$ to the set of multilinear maps into $P$. Different parenthesizations are connected by the unique isomorphism preserving pure tensors.

For $k=0$, take $T=R$ and identify zero-variable multilinear maps with chosen elements of $P$. For $k=1$, take $T=M_1$.

For every natural $n$, the function
$\operatorname{sgn}:S_n\to\{+1,-1\}$ is a group homomorphism. It is
surjective exactly when $n\ge2$; for $n=0$ and $n=1$ its image is $\{1\}$.

For $n\in\mathbb N$, the **alternating group** is the kernel of the sign
homomorphism,

$$A_n:=\ker(\operatorname{sgn}:S_n\to\{+1,-1\})=\{\sigma\in S_n:\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)=1\}.$$

Thus $A_n$ consists exactly of the even permutations. The subgroup and
normality assertions implicit in the word “group” follow from
[[thm-image-subgroup-and-kernel-normal]].

For $n\ge2$, the sign homomorphism is the unique nontrivial group homomorphism
$S_n\to\{+1,-1\}$.

derivations.claim: [Permutation isometries on the dense algebraic core] The span of iterated elementary tensors is dense in $H^{\otimes n}$, by induction on the completion construction [F1]. On the algebraic iterated tensor product, the multilinear assignment $(v_0,\ldots,v_{n-1})\mapsto v_{\pi^{-1}(0)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n-1)}$ induces a linear map by [F3]. It descends isometrically to its image in the completed tensor power: for elementary tensors $v=v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1}$ and $w=w_0\otimes\cdots\otimes w_{n-1}$, the inner product of their permuted images is $\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\langle v_{\pi^{-1}(k)},w_{\pi^{-1}(k)}\rangle=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\langle v_k,w_k\rangle=\langle v,w\rangle$ by [F1]. Sesquilinearity gives the same identity for finite linear combinations, so any algebraic relation with zero norm has zero-norm image. The isometry therefore extends uniquely by continuity to $U_\pi$ on the completion. For $n=1$ it is the identity, and the zero Hilbert space is included.

[Group law and unitarity] Direct substitution of indices in the elementary formula gives $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$ and $U_e=I$ on the dense algebraic core; continuity gives these equalities on the whole completion. Thus $U_{\pi^{-1}}U_\pi=I=U_\pi U_{\pi^{-1}}$, so the isometry of step 1.1 is surjective and unitary, with $U_\pi^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$. Any bounded operator with the same elementary action agrees with this one on a dense span and hence everywhere, proving uniqueness. No choice of permutation word or zeroth tensor power is needed.

[The projections are orthogonal projections] With coefficients $c_+(\pi)=1$ and $c_-(\pi)=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)$, write $P_\pm:=\frac1{n!}\sum_\pi c_\pm(\pi)U_\pi$ as in the Statement, use $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$ and reindex $\tau=\pi\sigma$: for $P_+$ this gives $P_+^2=\frac1{(n!)^2}\sum_{\pi,\sigma}U_{\pi\sigma}=\frac1{(n!)^2}\sum_\tau n!\,U_\tau=P_+$, and for $P_-$, since $\sigma=\pi^{-1}\tau$ and by [F4] $\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)=\operatorname{sgn}(\tau)$, it gives $P_-^2=\frac1{(n!)^2}\sum_{\pi,\sigma}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)U_{\pi\sigma}=\frac1{(n!)^2}\sum_\tau n!\,\operatorname{sgn}(\tau)U_\tau=P_-$; moreover $P_\pm^*=\frac1{n!}\sum_\pi c_\pm(\pi)U_{\pi^{-1}}=\frac1{n!}\sum_\tau c_\pm(\tau)U_\tau=P_\pm$ because $U_\pi^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(\pi^{-1})=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)$ [F4]. Hence $P_\pm$ are orthogonal projections.

[Ranges and transformation laws] For every $\pi$, $U_\pi P_+=\frac1{n!}\sum_\sigma U_{\pi\sigma}=\frac1{n!}\sum_\tau U_\tau=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=\frac1{n!}\sum_\sigma\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)U_{\pi\sigma}=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\frac1{n!}\sum_\tau\operatorname{sgn}(\tau)U_\tau=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$, using $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\operatorname{sgn}(\pi\sigma)=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)$ [F4]; by self-adjointness of the projections these identities also hold with the order reversed. Consequently, if $u\in\operatorname{ran}P_+$ then $U_\pi u=P_+u=u$ for all $\pi$, and if $u\in\operatorname{ran}P_-$ then $U_\pi u=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)u$; conversely $U_\pi u=u$ for all $\pi$ gives $P_+u=u$, and $U_\pi u=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)u$ for all $\pi$ gives $P_-u=\frac1{n!}\sum_\pi\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)^2u=u$.

[Vanishing on repeated factors] Suppose $v_i=v_j$ for distinct $i,j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ and let $\tau$ be the transposition swapping those positions. Then $U_\tau(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1}$ because the swap exchanges equal vectors. Pairing the terms of the sum defining $n!P_-$ as $\{\pi,\pi\tau\}$ over a set of coset representatives of the subgroup $\{e,\tau\}$ gives, for each pair, $\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi v+\operatorname{sgn}(\pi\tau)U_{\pi\tau}v=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi v-\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi U_\tau v=0$ by $U_{\pi\tau}=U_\pi U_\tau$ and $U_\tau v=v$. Hence $P_-v=0$ for the tensor with a repeated factor.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

For $[f],[g]\in L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$, the proposed pairing is
$$\langle[f],[g]\rangle:=\int_X f\overline g\,d\mu.$$
The integral is computed from measurable representatives. By [[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]], $\overline g\in L^2$ and $\int|f\overline g|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2<\infty$, so this representative expression is defined. The measurable and integration conventions are those of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. This fixes the **first-variable-linear** convention. The following theorem, named in `justified_by`, establishes class invariance and the inner-product axioms; the present definition does not assume that obligation.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the Lebesgue measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ is the completion of the product measure
$\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let
$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y
otin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and

2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $(X,\mathcal{A}_0,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$(X,\overline{\mathcal{A}_0},\overline{\mu})$ be its completion. If
$f : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is measurable with respect to
$\overline{\mathcal{A}_0}$, then there is an $\mathcal{A}_0$-measurable function
$g : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ such that $f=g$ almost everywhere.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $X$ be a set. A **pi-system on $X$** is a nonempty family
$\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ closed under binary intersections: if
$A,B\in\mathcal P$, then $A\cap B\in\mathcal P$.

The nonempty-family requirement is the convention used here. It does not require
$X\in\mathcal P$ and it does not add an empty-intersection axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. A subset of
$X \times Y$ is a **measurable rectangle** if it has the form $A \times B$ with
$A \in \mathcal A$ and $B \in \mathcal B$.

The ambient sigma-algebras matter: the same set may be a measurable rectangle
for one pair $(\mathcal A,\mathcal B)$ and not for another.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$. In the product topology on $\mathbb R^n$,
each of the following families generates $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)$: all open
sets; all closed sets; all compact sets; all Euclidean open balls; all open
boxes; all rational open boxes; and all rational half-open boxes
$\prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ with rational endpoints $a_i<b_i$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $X$ be a normed space, let $D \subseteq X$ be a dense normed subspace, let
$Y$ be a Banach space, and let $T:D\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator. Then
there is a unique bounded linear operator $\widetilde T:X\to Y$ such that

$$\widetilde T|_D = T,$$

and $\|\widetilde T\| = \|T\|$.

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Write $\beta_n$ for the restriction of $\lambda_n$ to
the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Then $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is exactly the
completion domain of $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n), \beta_n)$
([[def-completion-of-a-measure-space]]), and $\lambda_n$ is the completed measure
there. Explicitly,

$$E \in \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) \iff E = A\cup N \text{ for some } A, Z \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \text{ with } N \subseteq Z \text{ and } \beta_n(Z) = 0,$$

and then $\lambda_n(E) = \beta_n(A)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $(X,\mathcal{A}_0,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$(X,\overline{\mathcal{A}_0},\overline{\mu})$ be its completion. If
$f : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is measurable with respect to
$\overline{\mathcal{A}_0}$, then there is an $\mathcal{A}_0$-measurable function
$g : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ such that $f=g$ almost everywhere.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then

$$M^{\perp\perp}=\overline{M},$$

where $\overline M$ is the norm closure of $M$ and $M^{\perp\perp}=(M^\perp)^\perp$.

[Isometry on finite sums] For $f\in L^2(\lambda_a)$ and $g\in L^2(\lambda_b)$ choose measurable representatives. By [F2], replacing them by Borel representatives changes the product only on null strips in the completed product, and the product class is well defined. For finite sums $z=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_if_i\otimes g_i$ and $z'=\sum_{j=1}^m\beta_jf'_j\otimes g'_j$, each $f_i\overline{f'_j}\in L^1(\lambda_a)$ and $g_i\overline{g'_j}\in L^1(\lambda_b)$ by [F1], so the product is integrable in the completed product by Fubini [F2], and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^{a+b}}f_i(x)\overline{f'_j(x)}g_i(y)\overline{g'_j(y)}\,d\lambda_{a+b}(x,y)=\langle f_i,f'_j\rangle\langle g_i,g'_j\rangle.$$
The map $(f,g)\mapsto[f(x)g(y)]$ is bilinear, hence descends through the defining tensor relations to a linear map $\Theta_0$ on the algebraic tensor product. Summing with coefficients $\alpha_i\overline{\beta_j}$ gives $\langle\Theta_0z,\Theta_0z'\rangle=\langle z,z'\rangle$ by [F1]. Taking $z'=z$ gives $\Theta_0z=0\Rightarrow z=0$, so $\Theta_0$ is well defined and isometric on the dense algebraic tensor product.

[Finite-positive-measure uniqueness in the first variable] Let $h\in L^2(\mathbb R^{a+b})$ be orthogonal to every product of bounded-box indicators, so $\int_{B\times C}h=0$ for all boxes $B,C$. For each bounded rational half-open box $B\subseteq\mathbb R^b$, define $h_B(x):=\int_Bh(x,y)dy$ for a.e. $x$. Cauchy-Schwarz gives $|h_B(x)|^2\le|B|\int_B|h(x,y)|^2dy$, and Tonelli [F2] shows $h_B\in L^2(\mathbb R^a)$. Fubini [F2] gives $\int_Ch_B=\int_{C\times B}h=0$ for every rational half-open box $C\subseteq\mathbb R^a$. Fix a bounded rational half-open box $K\subseteq\mathbb R^a$ and write $u=\operatorname{Re}h_B$, $v=\operatorname{Im}h_B$. By [F5], choose Borel representatives $\widetilde u,\widetilde v$ equal a.e. to $u,v$. The family $\mathcal P_K:=\{K\cap C:C\text{ is a rational half-open box in }\mathbb R^a\}$ is a $\pi$-system containing $K$ and generating the relative Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $K$ by [F3]. The positive and negative parts $\widetilde u_+,\widetilde u_-,\widetilde v_+,\widetilde v_-$ are integrable on $K$ because $K$ has finite measure and $h_B\in L^2$. The finite positive Borel measures $A\mapsto\int_A\widetilde u_+$ and $A\mapsto\int_A\widetilde u_-$ agree on $\mathcal P_K$, including the total mass at $K$, since $\int_Au=0$ there; likewise the measures from $\widetilde v_+$ and $\widetilde v_-$ agree. By [F3] these equalities hold for every Borel $A\subseteq K$. Taking the Borel sets where $\widetilde u>0$, $\widetilde u<0$, $\widetilde v>0$ and $\widetilde v<0$ shows $u=v=0$ a.e. on $K$. The countable rational half-open boxes $K$ cover $\mathbb R^a$, so $h_B=0$ a.e. on $\mathbb R^a$ for each rational half-open $B$.

[Zero orthogonal complement] There are countably many rational half-open boxes $B\subseteq\mathbb R^b$, and step 1.2 gives $h_B=0$ a.e. for each; completed-product Fubini [F2] also gives $h(x,\cdot)\in L^2(\mathbb R^b)$ for a.e. $x$. Intersecting these countably many full-measure sets, for a.e. $x$ the section is in $L^2$ and $\int_Bh(x,y)dy=0$ for every rational half-open $B$. Fix such an $x$. On each bounded rational half-open box $K\subseteq\mathbb R^b$, choose Borel representatives of the real and imaginary parts of $h(x,\cdot)$ by [F5]. The positive and negative parts of these representatives define finite positive Borel measures on $K$; as in step 1.2 they agree on the $\pi$-system of rational half-open subboxes, including $K$, so [F3] makes the positive and negative measures equal on every Borel subset of $K$. Their positive and negative level sets then show the real and imaginary parts vanish a.e. on $K$. The countably many $K$ cover $\mathbb R^b$, hence $h(x,\cdot)=0$ a.e. for a.e. $x$, and Tonelli [F2] gives $h=0$ a.e. Thus $\operatorname{Ran}\Theta_0^\perp=\{0\}$; since $\operatorname{Ran}\Theta_0$ is a linear subspace, [F6] gives $\overline{\operatorname{Ran}\Theta_0}=\operatorname{Ran}\Theta_0^{\perp\perp}=L^2(\lambda_{a+b})$.

[Extension and surjectivity] By [F4], whose Banach-space hypothesis holds by Riesz–Fischer, the isometry $\Theta_0$ on the dense algebraic tensor product extends uniquely to a linear isometry $\Theta$ of the completion. Its range is closed (isometries have closed range: if $\Theta z_n\to w$ then $(z_n)$ is Cauchy, so $z_n\to z$ and $w=\Theta z$) and dense by step 2.1, hence is all of $L^2(\lambda_{a+b})$. Thus $\Theta$ is a surjective linear isometry, i.e. unitary, with the stated action on elementary tensors.

([[def-trace-class-operator]]) if and only if there are families
$(u_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $H$ and $(v_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $K$, indexed by the positive

$$\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<+\infty$$

infimum is attained: using its positive-integer index set and padding finite rank by zeros,

   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

derivations.claim: [Rank-one multiplication] For $x\in H$, $(BT_{u,v})x=B(\langle x,v\rangle u)=\langle x,v\rangle Bu=T_{Bu,v}x$, so $BT_{u,v}=T_{Bu,v}$; and $(T_{u,v}B)x=\langle Bx,v\rangle u=\langle x,B^*v\rangle u=T_{u,B^*v}x$ by [F5], so $T_{u,v}B=T_{u,B^*v}$. Both are bounded because $B$ is and the displayed maps have the stated form.

[Trace-norm convergence of the multiplier series] Write $T_n:=\sum_{j\le n}T_{u_j,v_j}$, so $\|T-T_n\|\to0$. Then $BT_n=\sum_{j\le n}T_{Bu_j,v_j}$ by step 1.1, and $\sum_j\|T_{Bu_j,v_j}\|_1=\sum_j\|Bu_j\|\,\|v_j\|\le\|B\|\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<\infty$ by [F1]; since the trace-class operators are complete in trace norm [F3], the series $\sum_jT_{Bu_j,v_j}$ converges in trace norm, and its limit agrees with $BT$ because trace-norm convergence implies operator-norm convergence and $BT_n\to BT$ in operator norm. Hence $BT=\sum_jT_{Bu_j,v_j}$ in trace norm, with $\|BT\|_1\le\|B\|\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|$.

[Trace of the left product] By [F4], $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\lim_n\operatorname{tr}(BT_n)=\lim_n\sum_{j\le n}\operatorname{tr}(T_{Bu_j,v_j})=\lim_n\sum_{j\le n}\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle$, because the trace is linear on the finite sums $BT_n$ and continuous for the trace norm, and $BT_n\to BT$ in trace norm by step 2.1. Thus $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\sum_j\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle$, and the series converges absolutely since $|\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle|=\bigl|\operatorname{tr}(T_{Bu_j,v_j})\bigr|\le\|Bu_j\|\,\|v_j\|$ by [F1]; the bound $\bigl|\operatorname{tr}(BT)\bigr|\le\|B\|\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|$ follows from [F4] and step 2.1.

[Right multiplication and cyclicity] By step 1.1, $T_nB=\sum_{j\le n}T_{u_j,B^*v_j}$, and $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|B^*v_j\|\le\|B\|\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<\infty$ by [F5]. Exactly as in step 2.1, trace-norm completeness gives convergence of this series to $TB$, since its operator-norm limit is $TB$. Trace continuity and the rank-one trace formula therefore give $\operatorname{tr}(TB)=\sum_j\langle u_j,B^*v_j\rangle$ with absolute convergence. Each summand equals $\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle$ by the adjoint identity, so step 3.1 gives $\operatorname{tr}(TB)=\operatorname{tr}(BT)$ for the original arbitrary nuclear representation. Every trace-class operator has such a representation by [F2]; the stated rank-one trace identity is [F1]. Only bounded multipliers were used.
