citations.quote:
Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb C$. The function $f$ is **complex differentiable at $a$** if the limit

$$ \lim_{\substack{h\to0\\ h\ne0,\ a+h\in U}}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} $$

exists in the metric of [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. Its value is the **complex derivative** of $f$ at $a$, denoted $f'(a)$. The increments are nonzero and remain in the domain; because $U$ is open, all sufficiently small increments are allowed.

The function $f$ is **holomorphic on $U$** when it is complex differentiable at every point of $U$. A function holomorphic on all of $\mathbb C$ is **entire**. The word analytic is reserved for the local power-series notion.

A **complex domain** is a nonempty, connected, open subset $U\subseteq\mathbb C$. Open means open in the modulus metric of [[def-metric-topology]], and connected has the meaning of [[def-connected-space]]. By [[rem-complex-plane-euclidean-dictionary]], these are exactly the usual Euclidean notions for the corresponding subset of $\mathbb R^2$.

For $z\ne0$ with principal polar form $z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$, $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$, define the **principal logarithm**
$$\operatorname{Log}z:=\log r+i\theta.$$
The set of all complex logarithms of $z$ is
$$\log_{\mathrm{multi}}z:=\{v\in\mathbb C:\exp v=z\}.$$
For $w\in\mathbb C$, define the **principal power** and the **multivalued power** respectively by
$$z^w_{\mathrm{pr}}:=\exp(w\operatorname{Log}z),\qquad z^w_{\mathrm{multi}}:=\{\exp(wv):v\in\log_{\mathrm{multi}}z\}.$$
Thus the first is one specified complex number and the second is a set of complex numbers; neither notation silently identifies them. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-polar-form-with-unique-principal-argument]], [[def-natural-logarithm]], [[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

Let $S=\mathbb C\setminus\{x\in\mathbb R:x\le0\}$ be the slit plane. Then $S$ is
a complex domain, star-shaped with respect to $1$, and homologically simply
connected. The principal logarithm $\operatorname{Log}$
([[def-complex-logarithms-principal-logarithm-and-complex-powers]]) is the
unique holomorphic $F:S\to\mathbb C$ with

$$\exp(F(z))=z\ \ (z\in S)\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(1)=0,$$

and it satisfies $\operatorname{Log}'(z)=1/z$ on $S$.

If two holomorphic functions on a complex domain agree on a set with an accumulation point in the domain, then they agree everywhere on the domain.

Precisely, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a complex domain ([[def-complex-domain]]), let $f,g:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose that some $a\in\Omega$ is an accumulation point of $\{z\in\Omega:f(z)=g(z)\}$. Then $f=g$ on $\Omega$. The requirement $a\in\Omega$ is essential.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Let $f$ be Riemann integrable on every compact interval $[a,R]$ with $R>a$. The improper integral over the right-unbounded interval is
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx:=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_a^R f(x)\,dx,$$
provided this limit exists as a finite real number. In that case the improper integral **converges**; otherwise it diverges. In particular, a limit of $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ is divergence, not convergence to an extended-real value.

If $f$ is Riemann integrable on every $[R,b]$ with $R<b$, define
$$\int_{-\infty}^b f(x)\,dx:=\lim_{R\to-\infty}\int_R^b f(x)\,dx$$
under the same finite-limit convention. All finite integrals use the oriented convention.

derivations.claim: [Absolute convergence] Let $z\in\Omega$ and $\delta:=\operatorname{Re}z>0$. For every $x$, $|e^{-z|x|^2}|=e^{-\delta|x|^2}$, whose integral over $\mathbb R^n$ is finite by [F1] with $s=\delta$; hence the real and imaginary parts of $x\mapsto e^{-z|x|^2}$ are absolutely improperly integrable and $G_n(z)$ is well defined by [F7]. The same bound holds uniformly on compact subsets of $\Omega$, where $\delta$ can be taken positive uniformly.

[Holomorphy of $G_1$] Fix $z\in\Omega$ and $0<\delta<\operatorname{Re}z$; let $|h|<\delta/2$. For the function $w\mapsto e^w$ the second-order Taylor remainder satisfies $|e^{w}-1-w|\le|w|^2e^{|w|}$ (the power series of $e^w-1-w$ has its first term $\frac{w^2}2$ and the remaining terms are bounded by $\frac{|w|^2}{2}(e^{|w|}-1)\le|w|^2e^{|w|}$). Applying this with $w=-hx^2$ gives $\bigl|e^{-zx^2}\frac{e^{-hx^2}-1+hx^2}{h}\bigr|\le|h|x^4e^{(|h|-\operatorname{Re}z)x^2}\le|h|x^4e^{-\delta x^2/2}$ for all real $x$ and all $|h|<\delta/2$, and $x\mapsto x^4e^{-\delta x^2/2}$ has finite integral; by [F2] (applied on $[-R,R]$ uniformly in $R$ and then by [F7]) the difference quotient $\bigl(G_1(z+h)-G_1(z)\bigr)/h$ tends, as $h\to0$, to $-\int_{\mathbb R}x^2e^{-zx^2}dx$. Hence $G_1$ is complex differentiable at every $z\in\Omega$, with the displayed derivative; by [F3] it is holomorphic on $\Omega$.

[The candidate branch] Put $H(z):=\sqrt\pi\,\exp\bigl(-\tfrac12\operatorname{Log}z\bigr)$ for $z$ in the slit plane $S\supseteq\Omega$. By [F4], $\operatorname{Log}$ is holomorphic on $S$ with $\operatorname{Log}'z=1/z$, and the complex exponential is entire with derivative itself, so by the chain rule for complex derivatives $H$ is holomorphic on the complex domain $S$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]], [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]); also $H(z)^2=\pi\exp(-\operatorname{Log}z)=\pi/z$ because $\exp(\operatorname{Log}z)=z$. On the positive axis, $\operatorname{Log}t=\ln t$ [F4], so $H(t)=\sqrt\pi\,t^{-1/2}=\sqrt{\pi/t}$, which equals $G_1(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-tx^2}dx$ by [F1] with $n=1$, $s=t$.

[Agreement by the identity theorem] The right half-plane $\Omega$ is nonempty, open and convex (if $\operatorname{Re}z_1,\operatorname{Re}z_2>0$ then $\operatorname{Re}((1-\lambda)z_1+\lambda z_2)>0$ for $0\le\lambda\le1$), hence a complex domain, and it is contained in $S$, so both $G_1$ (step 2.1) and $H$ (step 2.2) are holomorphic on $\Omega$. They agree at every $t>0$ (step 2.2), and the set $(0,\infty)$ has accumulation points in $\Omega$; by [F5] applied to the complex domain $\Omega$, $G_1=H$ on $\Omega$, giving clause (b).

[Factorization] For $z\in\Omega$ write $e^{-z|x|^2}=\prod_{j=1}^n e^{-zx_j^2}$; the absolute value factors as $\prod_je^{-\operatorname{Re}(z)x_j^2}$, a product of nonnegative integrable functions of the single coordinates. Tonelli's theorem [F6] applied to the nonnegative function $x\mapsto\prod_je^{-\operatorname{Re}(z)x_j^2}$ shows that the multiple integral of $|e^{-z|x|^2}|$ factorizes as the product of the one-dimensional integrals and is finite; hence $x\mapsto e^{-z|x|^2}$ is integrable on the product, and the Fubini theorem for $L^1$ functions ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]) applied to its real and imaginary parts gives $G_n(z)=\prod_{j=1}^nG_1(z)=G_1(z)^n$. By step 3.1, $G_1(z)^n=(\pi/z)^{n/2}$ in the branch notation of [F4]. This is clause (c), and $\operatorname{Re}(1+i\tau)=1>0$ shows the branch is defined at $1+i\tau$.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $X$ be a normed space, let $D \subseteq X$ be a dense normed subspace, let
$Y$ be a Banach space, and let $T:D\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator. Then
there is a unique bounded linear operator $\widetilde T:X\to Y$ such that

$$\widetilde T|_D = T,$$

and $\|\widetilde T\| = \|T\|$.

derivations.claim: [Absolute convergence and continuity] For $\psi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $|e^{-ip\cdot x/\hbar}\psi(x)|=|\psi(x)|$ is integrable by [F4], so the defining integral converges absolutely for every $p$ and $|\psi_p(p)|\le(2\pi\hbar)^{-d/2}\|\psi\|_1$. Continuity in $p$ follows from [F2] applied to $e^{-ip_n\cdot x/\hbar}\psi\to e^{-ip\cdot x/\hbar}\psi$ with the integrable dominating function $|\psi|$.

[Identification with the Plancherel transform] For $\psi\in\mathcal S$, put $\xi=p/(2\pi\hbar)$, so $2\pi x\cdot\xi=p\cdot x/\hbar$; comparing the defining integral of $\psi_p$ with the $L^1$ Fourier transform [F1] gives $\psi_p(p)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-d/2}\widehat\psi(\xi)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-d/2}\mathcal F_2\psi(p/(2\pi\hbar))$, the last equality because $\psi\in L^1$ and $\mathcal F_2$ extends $\widehat{\,\cdot\,}$. Hence $U_0=D_\hbar\circ\mathcal F_2$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$.

[The dilation is a unitary] For $g\in L^2$ the substitution $p=(2\pi\hbar)\xi$ is an invertible linear map with determinant $(2\pi\hbar)^d$, so by [F3] applied to $h=|g|^2$, $\int|D_\hbar g(p)|^2dp=(2\pi\hbar)^{-d}\int|g(p/(2\pi\hbar))|^2dp=(2\pi\hbar)^{-d}(2\pi\hbar)^d\int|g(\xi)|^2d\xi=\|g\|^2$. Thus $D_\hbar$ is a linear isometry; its inverse $D_\hbar^{-1}g(\xi)=(2\pi\hbar)^{d/2}g(2\pi\hbar\xi)$ is likewise an isometry and the two compositions are the identity, so $D_\hbar$ is a surjective isometry.

[Norm preservation on Schwartz functions] By steps 2.1 and 2.2 and unitarity of $\mathcal F_2$ [F1], $\|\psi_p\|_2=\|D_\hbar\mathcal F_2\psi\|_2=\|\mathcal F_2\psi\|_2=\|\psi\|_2$ for $\psi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$; moreover $U_0$ is linear on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ because the integral and the dilation are linear.

[Unique unitary extension] The subspace $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ is dense in $L^2$ because it contains the dense subspace $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ [F4]; by [F5] the isometry $U_0$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ has a unique bounded linear extension $U:L^2(\mathbb R^d,dx)\to L^2(\mathbb R^d,dp)$ with the same norm, so $\|U\psi\|=\|\psi\|$ for every $\psi\in L^2$. Surjectivity: for arbitrary $h\in L^2(\mathbb R^d,dp)$, the vector $\psi:=\mathcal F_2^*D_\hbar^{-1}h$ lies in $L^2$, and since $U$ agrees with $D_\hbar\mathcal F_2$ on the dense set $\mathcal S$ while both sides are bounded, $U\psi=h$; hence $U$ is onto. The norm identity of clause (c) is exactly $\|U\psi\|_2=\|\psi\|_2$, and the normalization discussion is the determinant computation of step 2.2 read at $g=\mathcal F_2\psi$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and for $u,v\in H$ let $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) For every bounded $B\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]),

$$BT_{u,v}=T_{Bu,v},\qquad T_{u,v}B=T_{u,B^*v},$$

with the Hilbert adjoint $B^*$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class and let $T=\sum_jT_{u_j,v_j}$ be a nuclear representation, i.e. the partial sums converge to $T$ in operator norm and $\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<\infty$ ([[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then for every bounded $B$

$$\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\sum_j\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(TB)=\sum_j\langle u_j,B^*v_j\rangle,$$

both series converging absolutely with $\bigl|\operatorname{tr}(BT)\bigr|\le\|B\|\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|$, and $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). In particular $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ for every trace-class $T$ and bounded $B$, and $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\langle u,v\rangle$. No cyclic permutation of unbounded operators is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and $K$
be Hilbert spaces over the same real or complex scalar field and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]). Then $T$ is trace class
([[def-trace-class-operator]]) if and only if there are families
$(u_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $H$ and $(v_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $K$, indexed by the positive
integers, with
$$\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<+\infty$$
such that the zero-based sequence of finite-rank operators defined by $R_0=0$
and
$$R_m:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\langle\cdot,u_j\rangle v_j\qquad(m\ge1)$$
converges to $T$ in operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]],
[[def-metric-convergence]]).  Here the displayed scalar series is, under the
library convention, the series of the sequence
$(\|u_{m+1}\|\,\|v_{m+1}\|)_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case
$$\|T\|_1=\inf\Bigl\{\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|:\ R_m\to T\ \text{in operator norm}\Bigr\},$$
the infimum being over all such **nuclear representations** of $T$, with the
same zero-based shift understood in every displayed sum, and the
infimum is attained: using its positive-integer index set and padding finite rank by zeros,
the singular-value series
$T=\sum_{j\in J}s_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ is a nuclear representation with
sum $\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and for $u,v\in H$ let $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

Then for every bounded $B$

In particular $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ for every trace-class $T$ and bounded $B$, and $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\langle u,v\rangle$. No cyclic permutation of unbounded operators is asserted.

Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a
sequence in $H$ whose range $\{x_n : n\in\mathbb N\}$ is dense in $H$
([[def-dense-top]]), and let

$$L_0:=\varnothing,\qquad L_{n+1}:=L_n\cup\Bigl\{\tfrac{v_n}{\|v_n\|}\Bigr\}\ \text{ if }\ v_n:=x_n-\sum_{e\in L_n}\langle x_n,e\rangle e\ne0, \qquad L_{n+1}:=L_n\ \text{ otherwise}.$$

Then $L:=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}L_n$ is a finite or countably infinite orthonormal
set whose closed linear span is $H$; that is, $L$ is an orthonormal basis of $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
it is obtained from the given sequence by Gram–Schmidt elimination. The
enumeration of $L$ is the canonical one by the stage at which an element
appears, and no choice principle is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,H',K,K'$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let $S\in\mathcal B(H,H')$, $T\in\mathcal B(K,K')$ be bounded linear operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Write $H\widehat\otimes K$ for the completion of the algebraic tensor product constructed in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], with inclusion $\kappa$.

(a) There is a unique bounded linear operator $S\otimes T: H\widehat\otimes K\to H'\widehat\otimes K'$ with $(S\otimes T)\kappa(u\otimes v)=\kappa'(Su\otimes Tv)$ for all $u\in H$, $v\in K$, and it satisfies $\|S\otimes T\|\le\|S\|\,\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]).

(b) For Hilbert spaces $H'',K''$ and bounded $S':H''\to H$, $T':K''\to K$, one has $(S\otimes T)(S'\otimes T')=(SS')\otimes(TT')$. In particular, for endomorphisms $S:H\to H$, $T:K\to K$, the endomorphisms $S\otimes I_K$ and $I_H\otimes T$ commute and their composite is $S\otimes T$.

(c) The Hilbert adjoint ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]) is $(S\otimes T)^*=S^*\otimes T^*$.

(d) If $S,T$ are unitary, then so is $S\otimes T$. No extension of unbounded maps, and no algebraic manipulation of domains of unbounded operators, is asserted.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: [The rank-one values] For $T_{u\otimes v,u'\otimes v'}$ and bounded $A$, $T(A\otimes I)=T_{u\otimes v,(A\otimes I)^*(u'\otimes v')}=T_{u\otimes v,A^*u'\otimes v'}$ by [F1], whose trace is $\langle u\otimes v,A^*u'\otimes v'\rangle=\langle u,A^*u'\rangle\langle v,v'\rangle=\langle Au,u'\rangle\langle v,v'\rangle$. On the other hand $\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\langle v,v'\rangle T_{u,u'})A\bigr)=\langle v,v'\rangle\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,u'}A)=\langle v,v'\rangle\langle Au,u'\rangle$ by [F1]. Hence the assignment $\operatorname{Tr}_KT_{u\otimes v,u'\otimes v'}:=\langle v,v'\rangle T_{u,u'}$ satisfies the defining identity on rank-one tensors, and $\|\operatorname{Tr}_KT_{u\otimes v,u'\otimes v'}\|_1\le\|v\|\,\|v'\|\,\|u\|\,\|u'\|=\|u\otimes v\|\,\|u'\otimes v'\|$ by [F1].

[Arbitrary rank-one vectors] Fix $w,z\in H\widehat\otimes K$. By density and Countable Choice choose sequences of finite algebraic tensors converging to these two vectors; collect their countably many second-factor vectors and let $K_0$ be their closed linear span. Finite rational complex combinations form an explicit dense sequence in $K_0$, so [F4] provides a finite/countable orthonormal basis $(f_b)$ of $K_0$. The maps taking $\sum_i u_i\otimes v_i$ to $\sum_i\langle v_i,f_b\rangle u_i$ have norm at most one by orthogonal coordinates and extend to the completion. Their values $w_b,z_b\in H$ satisfy $w=\sum_bw_b\otimes f_b$, $z=\sum_bz_b\otimes f_b$ and $\sum_b\|w_b\|^2=\|w\|^2$, $\sum_b\|z_b\|^2=\|z\|^2$: the finite-coordinate projections are contractions, converge on algebraic tensors in $H\odot K_0$, and hence converge on its closure, which contains $w,z$. Define $Q(w,z):=\sum_bT_{w_b,z_b}$. By [F1], [F2] and Cauchy–Schwarz, this converges in trace norm and $\|Q(w,z)\|_1\le\sum_b\|w_b\|\|z_b\|\le\|w\|\|z\|$. Finite-coordinate truncations and step 1.1 give $\operatorname{tr}(Q(w,z)A)=\langle(A\otimes I)w,z\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(T_{w,z}(A\otimes I))$; rank-one trace-norm continuity and bounded tensor maps [F4] pass this identity to limits. The identity uniquely determines $Q(w,z)$ by [F3], so it is independent of the supports, basis and approximants, is sesquilinear in $w,z$, and agrees with the elementary assignment.

[Extension to trace class] For a nuclear representation $T=\sum_jT_{w_j,z_j}$, define $\operatorname{Tr}_KT:=\sum_jQ(w_j,z_j)$. Step 2.1 and [F2] give trace-norm convergence and the bound $\|\operatorname{Tr}_KT\|_1\le\inf\sum_j\|w_j\|\|z_j\|=\|T\|_1$. The defining trace pairing follows by summing that of step 2.1, using trace-norm continuity and $\|A\otimes I\|\le\|A\|$. If two nuclear representations are used, both images have the same pairings against every bounded $A$, and their difference vanishes by [F3]. Thus the definition is independent of representation. The same uniqueness proves linearity, since the sum and scalar multiple of images satisfy the pairing for the sum and scalar multiple of inputs. This proves (a) and the elementary formula (c).

[Positivity and trace preservation] Step 2.1 gives $Q(w,w)=\sum_bT_{w_b,w_b}$, which is self-adjoint positive since $\langle T_{w_b,w_b}x,x\rangle=|\langle x,w_b\rangle|^2\ge0$ and trace-norm convergence implies operator-norm convergence. Every self-adjoint positive trace-class input of positive trace becomes a density operator after division by its trace, so it has the positive spectral rank-one expansion of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]; a zero-trace self-adjoint positive trace-class input is zero by [[thm-trace-of-a-positive-operator-is-the-sum-of-its-eigenvalues]]. The bounded map of step 3.1 carries the partial sums of this expansion to positive sums of the corresponding $Q(w,w)$ and hence carries its limit to a self-adjoint positive operator. Taking $A=I_H$ in the defining pairing gives $\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Tr}_KT=\operatorname{tr}T$. Hence density operators map to density operators.

[Uniqueness] If two linear maps $\operatorname{Tr}_K,\operatorname{Tr}_K'$ satisfy the defining identity for all $T$ and $A$, then for fixed $T$ the difference $S=\operatorname{Tr}_KT-\operatorname{Tr}_K'T$ satisfies $\operatorname{tr}(SA)=0$ for all bounded $A$, so $S=0$ by [F3]. Hence the map is unique and, in particular, independent of any basis; the symmetrically defined $\operatorname{Tr}_H$ has the stated identity.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Here $|A|^{1/2}$ denotes the unbounded PVM integral $f(E_A)$ for $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{1/2}$, with domain $D(f(E_A))=\{\psi:\int |\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty\}$ as in [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$

   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and $K$
be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $E$ be a Hilbert
basis of $H$ and $G$ a Hilbert basis of $K$ (both supplied as data), and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be compact ([[def-compact-linear-operator]]). Then:

1. **(factorization of a trace-class operator)** if $T$ is trace class
   ([[def-trace-class-operator]]), then, with $|T|$, $U$ and the singular system
   of $T$ ([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]],
   [[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]), the operators
   $$B:=|T|^{1/2}\in\mathcal B(H),\qquad A:=U|T|^{1/2}\in\mathcal B(H,K)$$
   satisfy $T=AB$, are both Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$
   ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]), and
   $$\|A\|_{HS,E}=\|B\|_{HS,E}=\|T\|_1^{1/2},$$
   so that $\|A\|_{HS,E}\|B\|_{HS,E}=\|T\|_1$: the trace norm is attained by this
   factorization;
2. **(products of Hilbert–Schmidt operators are trace class)** conversely, if
   there are a real or complex Hilbert space $H_0$ with a supplied Hilbert basis
   $E_0$, a Hilbert–Schmidt operator $B\in\mathcal B(H,H_0)$ relative to $E$ and a
   Hilbert–Schmidt operator $A\in\mathcal B(H_0,K)$ relative to $E_0$ with
   $T=AB$, then $T$ is trace class and
   $$\|T\|_1\le\|A\|_{HS,E_0}\|B\|_{HS,E};$$
   in particular $AB$ is compact and $\|T\|\le\|A\|_{HS,E_0}\|B\|_{HS,E}$.

The bases $E$, $E_0$, $G$ are supplied data; no existence of a Hilbert basis is
asserted or used, and the adjoint-stability of the Hilbert–Schmidt norm across

derivations.claim: [Norm identity, including the zero space] If $H=\{0\}$, then every $M_a$ and every trace-class input is zero, so the unique map on $\mathcal S_1(H)=\{0\}$ satisfies (a)-(c). Suppose henceforth that $H\ne\{0\}$. For every $x$, $\sum_{a\le N}\|M_ax\|^2$ is the increasing sequence $\langle(\sum_{a\le N}M_a^*M_a)x,x\rangle$, so its supremum is $\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2$ by strong convergence and continuity of the inner product in $N$; by [F1] this supremum is $\sum_a\|M_ax\|^2$.

[Positive input] Let $\rho=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ be the spectral expansion [F3]. The partial sums $\Phi_N(\rho):=\sum_{a\le N}M_a\rho M_a^*$ are positive trace-class with $\operatorname{tr}\Phi_N(\rho)=\sum_{a\le N}\sum_nw_n\|M_au_n\|^2$ by [F2]; the double sum increases with $N$, and its limit is $\sum_nw_n\sum_a\|M_au_n\|^2=\sum_nw_n\|u_n\|^2=\operatorname{tr}\rho$ by step 1.1 and Tonelli for nonnegative series. Hence the increasing positive sequence $\Phi_N(\rho)$ has traces increasing to $\operatorname{tr}\rho$, so for $N\ge M$ we have $\|\Phi_N(\rho)-\Phi_M(\rho)\|_1=\operatorname{tr}\Phi_N(\rho)-\operatorname{tr}\Phi_M(\rho)\to0$ ([F4] with positivity of the difference); by completeness of $\mathcal S_1(H)$ [F2] the series converges in trace norm to a trace-class $\Phi(\rho)\ge0$ (the trace-norm limit of positive operators is positive) with $\operatorname{tr}\Phi(\rho)=\operatorname{tr}\rho$.

[Linear extension by nuclear convergence] For rank-one input, $M_aT_{u,v}M_a^*=T_{M_au,M_av}$ by [F2]. Step 1.1 and Cauchy–Schwarz give $\sum_a\|M_au\|\|M_av\|\le\|u\|\|v\|$. Thus for a nuclear input $T=\sum_jT_{u_j,v_j}$ the double series of Kraus rank-one images is absolutely summable in trace norm, with total norm at most $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|$. Its sum is the trace-norm limit of $\Phi_N(T)=\sum_{a\le N}M_aTM_a^*$, by interchanging absolutely convergent sums and the bounded two-sided ideal action. This limit depends only on $T$, so defines a linear map $\Phi$ extending the positive-input map of step 2.1. Taking the nuclear infimum ([[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]]) gives the bound $\|\Phi(T)\|_1\le\|T\|_1$ for every input. For rank-one inputs, the trace sum is $\sum_a\langle M_au,M_av\rangle=\langle u,v\rangle$, by strong completeness and the adjoint identity; extending through the absolutely convergent nuclear sum proves $\operatorname{tr}\Phi(T)=\operatorname{tr}T$. The positive trace-class operators linearly span trace class by the self-adjoint real/imaginary and positive/negative spectral decompositions in [F4], so no other linear extension agreeing with step 2.1 is possible.

[Norm bound and conclusion] For self-adjoint $\rho$ with spectral decomposition $\rho=\rho^+-\rho^-$ write $T=\rho$. Then $\Phi(\rho)=\Phi(\rho^+)-\Phi(\rho^-)$ by construction, so $\|\Phi(\rho)\|_1\le\operatorname{tr}\Phi(\rho^+)+\operatorname{tr}\Phi(\rho^-)=\operatorname{tr}\rho^++\operatorname{tr}\rho^-=\|\rho\|_1$ using step 2.1 and [F4]. Positivity for arbitrary $\rho\ge0$ is step 2.1, and trace preservation was shown in step 3.1; hence density operators map to density operators.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,H',K,K'$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let $S\in\mathcal B(H,H')$, $T\in\mathcal B(K,K')$ be bounded linear operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Write $H\widehat\otimes K$ for the completion of the algebraic tensor product constructed in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], with inclusion $\kappa$.

(a) There is a unique bounded linear operator $S\otimes T: H\widehat\otimes K\to H'\widehat\otimes K'$ with $(S\otimes T)\kappa(u\otimes v)=\kappa'(Su\otimes Tv)$ for all $u\in H$, $v\in K$, and it satisfies $\|S\otimes T\|\le\|S\|\,\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]).

(b) For Hilbert spaces $H'',K''$ and bounded $S':H''\to H$, $T':K''\to K$, one has $(S\otimes T)(S'\otimes T')=(SS')\otimes(TT')$. In particular, for endomorphisms $S:H\to H$, $T:K\to K$, the endomorphisms $S\otimes I_K$ and $I_H\otimes T$ commute and their composite is $S\otimes T$.

(c) The Hilbert adjoint ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]) is $(S\otimes T)^*=S^*\otimes T^*$.

(d) If $S,T$ are unitary, then so is $S\otimes T$. No extension of unbounded maps, and no algebraic manipulation of domains of unbounded operators, is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and for $u,v\in H$ let $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) For every bounded $B\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]),

$$BT_{u,v}=T_{Bu,v},\qquad T_{u,v}B=T_{u,B^*v},$$

with the Hilbert adjoint $B^*$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class and let $T=\sum_jT_{u_j,v_j}$ be a nuclear representation, i.e. the partial sums converge to $T$ in operator norm and $\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<\infty$ ([[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then for every bounded $B$

$$\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\sum_j\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(TB)=\sum_j\langle u_j,B^*v_j\rangle,$$

both series converging absolutely with $\bigl|\operatorname{tr}(BT)\bigr|\le\|B\|\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|$, and $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). In particular $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ for every trace-class $T$ and bounded $B$, and $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\langle u,v\rangle$. No cyclic permutation of unbounded operators is asserted.

and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $(M_a)_{a\ge1}$ be bounded operators on $H$ with $\sum_{a\le N}M_a^*M_a\to I$ strongly, and let $\Phi(\rho)=\sum_aM_a\rho M_a^*$ be the map of [[lem-nrqm-composites-countable-kraus-normalization]]. Here a map on trace-class operators is **completely positive on finite-dimensional ancillas** when, for every finite-dimensional complex inner product space $C$, its matrixwise amplification $I_C\otimes\Phi$ preserves self-adjoint positive trace-class operators on $C\widehat\otimes H$. Then for every finite-dimensional complex inner product space $C$ the amplification

$$I_C\otimes\Phi:S_1(C\widehat\otimes H)\to S_1(C\widehat\otimes H)$$

is well defined by the trace-norm convergent series $\sum_a(I_C\otimes M_a)R(I_C\otimes M_a^*)$ and preserves positivity: every self-adjoint positive trace-class $R$ (positivity in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]) has $I_C\otimes\Phi(R)$ self-adjoint positive. Hence $\Phi$ is completely positive on every finite-dimensional ancilla in the stated sense.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,K$ be nonzero complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $H\widehat\otimes K$ be their completed tensor product ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]); write $T_{x,z}x'=\langle x',z\rangle x$ for rank-one operators ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]) and $\operatorname{tr}$ for the trace of a trace-class operator ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]).

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_KT)A\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(T(A\otimes I_K)\bigr)$$

for every trace-class $T$ and every $A\in\mathcal B(H)$; it satisfies $\|\operatorname{Tr}_KT\|_1\le\|T\|_1$ and is independent of any chosen orthonormal basis of $K$.

(b) $\operatorname{Tr}_K$ maps self-adjoint positive trace-class operators to self-adjoint positive trace-class operators (positivity in the bounded-operator sense of [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]), is trace preserving ($\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Tr}_KT=\operatorname{tr}T$), and maps density operators to density operators ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]).

derivations.claim: [Convergence of the local map] If $H=\{0\}$ or $K=\{0\}$, then $R=0$ and every summand $(I_H\otimes M_a)R(I_H\otimes M_a)^*$ is zero; hence $\Phi(R)=0$ and both sides of $\operatorname{Tr}_K\Phi(R)=\operatorname{Tr}_KR$ are zero by the convention in the Statement. Assume henceforth $H,K\ne\{0\}$. By [F1] the amplified family satisfies the strong completeness hypothesis of [F2] on the Hilbert space $H\widehat\otimes K$, so the series $\sum_aV_aRV_a^*$ with $V_a=I_H\otimes M_a$ converges in trace norm, its sum $\Phi(R)$ is trace class with $\operatorname{tr}\Phi(R)=\operatorname{tr}R$, and $\Phi(R)\ge0$ for $R\ge0$.

[Pairing computation] For bounded $A$ and $V_a=I_H\otimes M_a$, cyclicity [F4] gives $\operatorname{tr}\bigl(V_aRV_a^*(A\otimes I_K)\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\,V_a^*(A\otimes I_K)V_a\bigr)$ with $V_a^*(A\otimes I_K)V_a=(I_H\otimes M_a^*)(A\otimes I_K)(I_H\otimes M_a)=A\otimes M_a^*M_a$. For each $N$, sum this identity over $a\le N$; trace-norm convergence of the series in step 1.1 and trace-norm continuity of the bounded trace pairing [F4] give $\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(R)(A\otimes I_K))=\lim_{N\to\infty}\operatorname{tr}(R(A\otimes S_N))$, where $S_N=\sum_{a\le N}M_a^*M_a$.

[Passing to the limit in the completeness sum] Let $R=\sum_jT_{w_j,z_j}$ be nuclear. For each $N$, $\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R(A\otimes\sum_{a\le N}M_a^*M_a)\bigr)=\sum_j\langle w_j,(A\otimes S_N)^*z_j\rangle$ with $S_N:=\sum_{a\le N}M_a^*M_a$, an absolutely convergent series with $|\langle w_j,(A\otimes S_N)^*z_j\rangle|\le\|A\|\,\|w_j\|\,\|z_j\|$; since $(A\otimes S_N)^*\to A^*\otimes I$ strongly, each term converges to $\langle w_j,(A^*\otimes I)z_j\rangle$, and the summable majorant gives $\sum_j\langle w_j,(A\otimes S_N)^*z_j\rangle\to\sum_j\langle w_j,(A^*\otimes I)z_j\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(R(A\otimes I_K))$. Hence $\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(R)(A\otimes I_K))=\operatorname{tr}(R(A\otimes I_K))$.

[Conclusion] By [F3], $\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_K\Phi(R))A\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(R)(A\otimes I_K))=\operatorname{tr}(R(A\otimes I_K))=\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{Tr}_KR)A)$ for every bounded $A$; since the pairings with all $A$ determine a trace-class operator by the uniqueness in [F3], $\operatorname{Tr}_K\Phi(R)=\operatorname{Tr}_KR$. The statement for the first factor is obtained by exchanging the roles of $H$ and $K$.

derivations.claim: [Countable supports and coefficients] By density and Countable Choice choose algebraic tensors $\Psi_n\to\Psi$ with finite factor decompositions. Their countably many factor vectors span closed subspaces $H_0,K_0$ with explicit dense sequences of finite rational complex combinations; [F1] supplies finite/countable orthonormal bases. The inclusion of $H_0\odot K_0$ in $H\widehat\otimes K$ is isometric and extends to its closed completion, which contains $\Psi$. Choose the basis $(f_j)$ of $K_0$. As in the orthogonal contraction construction of [[lem-nrqm-composites-separable-partial-trace]], coefficient contractions define $h_j\in H_0$ with $\Psi=\sum_jh_j\otimes f_j$ and $\sum_j\|h_j\|^2=\|\Psi\|^2$. All sums here may be finite or empty, including $\Psi=0$.

[The typed compact coefficient operator] Define $C(\sum_jz_j\bar f_j):=\sum_jz_jh_j$ first on finite sums in $\overline{K_0}$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|Cz\|\le(\sum_j\|h_j\|^2)^{1/2}\|z\|$, so it extends to all of $\overline{K_0}$ by continuity and completeness. The finite truncations $C_N$ have finite rank and $\|C-C_N\|\le(\sum_{j>N}\|h_j\|^2)^{1/2}\to0$, so [F2] makes $C$ compact. The adjoint has the correctly typed formula $C^*x=\sum_j\langle x,h_j\rangle\bar f_j$ for $x\in H_0$, hence $CC^*x=\sum_j\langle x,h_j\rangle h_j$. The finite sums $\sum_{j\le N}T_{h_j,h_j}$ converge in trace norm by [F4], with trace sum $\sum_j\|h_j\|^2$; their operator-norm limit is $CC^*$, so $CC^*$ is positive trace class with $\operatorname{tr}CC^*=\|\Psi\|^2$.

[Reduced-state identity] Let $\Psi_N=\sum_{j\le N}h_j\otimes f_j$. The elementary partial-trace formula gives $\operatorname{Tr}_KT_{\Psi_N,\Psi_N}=\sum_{j\le N}T_{h_j,h_j}$, regarding the latter operators on $H$ as zero on $H_0^\perp$. Rank-one continuity and boundedness of the partial trace [F4] pass to the limit and give $\operatorname{Tr}_KT_{\Psi,\Psi}=CC^*$ extended by zero. Thus the nonzero eigenvalues of $CC^*$ are intrinsic to $\Psi$, independent of all auxiliary supports and bases.

[Singular vectors in the conjugate factor] By [F3] choose orthonormal eigenvectors $v_r\in H_0$ for the positive eigenvalues $s_r^2$ of $CC^*$, counted with multiplicity; finite-dimensional eigenspace bases are supplied by [F1] and their countable selection uses the stated Countable Choice. Define $\bar u_r:=s_r^{-1}C^*v_r\in\overline{K_0}$. Then $\langle\bar u_r,\bar u_t\rangle=s_r^{-1}s_t^{-1}\langle v_r,CC^*v_t\rangle=\delta_{rt}$, so the actual vectors $u_r\in K_0$ are orthonormal too. By step 2.1 their coefficients obey $u_r=\sum_js_r^{-1}\langle h_j,v_r\rangle f_j$. The trace formula [F3] gives $\sum_rs_r^2=\operatorname{tr}CC^*=\|\Psi\|^2$, and infinitely many positive eigenvalues tend to zero.

[Reconstruction] If $g\in\ker CC^*$ then $0=\langle CC^*g,g\rangle=\|C^*g\|^2$, so all $\langle g,h_j\rangle$ vanish. Thus every $h_j$ is in the closed span of the $v_r$ by [F3], and $h_j=\sum_r\langle h_j,v_r\rangle v_r$. The orthonormal series $\sum_rs_rv_r\otimes u_r$ converges in tensor norm because $\sum_rs_r^2<\infty$. Its $f_j$ coefficient is $\sum_rs_r\langle u_r,f_j\rangle v_r=\sum_r\langle h_j,v_r\rangle v_r=h_j$ by step 4.1. The orthogonal coefficient norm formula [F1] therefore identifies its sum with $\Psi$. If $\Psi=0$, the positive spectrum and the Schmidt family are empty, giving the zero expansion.

[Purity and product criterion] For $\|\Psi\|=1$, steps 3.1–5.1 show that the reduced density has eigenvalues $s_r^2$ and $\sum_rs_r^2=1$, hence $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2=\sum_rs_r^4$. The difference $(\sum_rs_r^2)^2-\sum_rs_r^4=2\sum_{r<t}s_r^2s_t^2$ vanishes exactly when there is one positive coefficient. That case makes the expansion a product vector. Conversely for a nonzero product $a\otimes b$, its coefficients are $h_j=\langle b,f_j\rangle a$, so $C$ has rank one and $CC^*$ has one positive eigenvalue; for a unit product its reduced purity is one. All ambient Hilbert spaces remain arbitrary; only the supports of this particular vector were made countable. This establishes every claimed clause.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and for $u,v\in H$ let $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) For every bounded $B\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]),

$$BT_{u,v}=T_{Bu,v},\qquad T_{u,v}B=T_{u,B^*v},$$

with the Hilbert adjoint $B^*$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class and let $T=\sum_jT_{u_j,v_j}$ be a nuclear representation, i.e. the partial sums converge to $T$ in operator norm and $\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<\infty$ ([[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then for every bounded $B$

$$\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\sum_j\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(TB)=\sum_j\langle u_j,B^*v_j\rangle,$$

both series converging absolutely with $\bigl|\operatorname{tr}(BT)\bigr|\le\|B\|\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|$, and $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). In particular $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ for every trace-class $T$ and bounded $B$, and $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\langle u,v\rangle$. No cyclic permutation of unbounded operators is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Here $|A|^{1/2}$ denotes the unbounded PVM integral $f(E_A)$ for $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{1/2}$, with domain $D(f(E_A))=\{\psi:\int |\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty\}$ as in [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

derivations.claim: [The functional and its sesquilinear form] Fix $B\in\Sigma$. The map $f_B(T):=\operatorname{tr}(J_B(T))$ is a bounded linear functional on $\mathcal S_1(H)$ with $|f_B(T)|\le\|J_B\|\,\|T\|_1$ by [F2]. Define $b_B(u,v):=f_B(T_{u,v})$ on rank-one operators. Because $T_{u,v}$ is linear in $u$ and conjugate-linear in $v$ and $f_B$ is linear, $b_B$ is sesquilinear; by [F1], $|b_B(u,v)|\le\|J_B\|\,\|u\|\,\|v\|$.

[The effect] For fixed $u$, Riesz representation of $v\mapsto\overline{b_B(u,v)}$ gives a unique vector $F_Bu$ with $b_B(u,v)=\langle F_Bu,v\rangle$; the sesquilinear bound in step 1.1 makes $u\mapsto F_Bu$ a bounded linear operator. By [F4], $J_B(T_{u,u})$ is self-adjoint positive trace class and has nonnegative trace, so $b_B(u,u)\ge0$. The complement relation $J_X=J_B+J_{X\setminus B}$ and positivity of $J_{X\setminus B}$ give $b_B(u,u)\le b_X(u,u)=\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,u})=\|u\|^2$. Thus the diagonal form values are real, so polarization makes $b_B$ Hermitian and $F_B$ self-adjoint; the two inequalities show it is an effect in the stated sense. Linearity and trace-norm continuity [F1, F2] extend $\operatorname{tr}(J_B(T_{u,v}))=\langle F_Bu,v\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v}F_B)$ to every trace-class $T$. Uniqueness follows because all pairings $\langle F_Bu,v\rangle$ are fixed. This is (a).

[Normalization and countable additivity] For $T=T_{u,v}$ and $B=X$ the trace-preservation clause of the instrument gives $\langle F_Xu,v\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(J_X(T_{u,v}))=\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\langle u,v\rangle$, so $F_X=I$. For pairwise disjoint $B_n$ with union $B$, the instrument's countable additivity says $\sum_{n\le N}J_{B_n}(T)\to J_B(T)$ in trace norm; by linearity and trace-norm continuity of the functional $\operatorname{tr}(\cdot\,F_B)$-pairing [F1, F2], $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v}F_B)=\operatorname{tr}(J_B(T_{u,v}))=\lim_N\sum_{n\le N}\operatorname{tr}(J_{B_n}(T_{u,v}))=\sum_n\langle F_{B_n}u,v\rangle$ by step 2.1. As $u,v$ are arbitrary, this is $\langle F_Bu,v\rangle=\sum_n\langle F_{B_n}u,v\rangle$, which is (b).

[Heisenberg dual] Fix $B$ and bounded $A$. Define $c_A(u,v):=\operatorname{tr}(J_B(T_{u,v})A)$. This is sesquilinear in $(u,v)$ with $|c_A(u,v)|\le\|J_B\|\,\|A\|\,\|u\|\,\|v\|$ by [F1, F2]; by the Riesz construction in [F3] there is a unique bounded $J_B^*(A)$ with $c_A(u,v)=\langle J_B^*(A)u,v\rangle$ and $\|J_B^*(A)\|\le\|J_B\|\,\|A\|$. Then for rank-one $T_{u,v}$, $\operatorname{tr}(J_B(T_{u,v})A)=\langle J_B^*(A)u,v\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v}J_B^*(A))$ by [F1]; both sides are linear and trace-norm continuous in $T$ [F2], so the identity holds for all trace-class $T$. Linearity of $A\mapsto J_B^*(A)$ follows by uniqueness of the representing operator. If $A\ge0$ and $x\in H$, then $\langle J_B^*(A)x,x\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(J_B(T_{x,x})A)\ge0$: by [F4], $J_B(T_{x,x})=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ with $w_n\ge0$, and the trace is $\sum_nw_n\langle Au_n,u_n\rangle$, a convergent nonnegative sum. Its diagonal values are real, so polarization also gives $J_B^*(A)^*=J_B^*(A)$. Finally $J_X^*(I)=I$ by $\operatorname{tr}(J_X(T)I)=\operatorname{tr}T=\operatorname{tr}(TI)$ and uniqueness. This is (c).

[Probabilities] For a density operator $\rho=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$, step 2.1 gives $p(B)=\operatorname{tr}(J_B(\rho))=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_B)=\sum_nw_n\langle F_Bu_n,u_n\rangle$. Since $0\le F_B\le I$, each diagonal term lies in $[0,1]$ and $\sum_nw_n=1$, so $p(B)\in[0,1]$. Trace-norm additivity of $J$ and trace continuity imply countable additivity of $p$, and $p(X)=1$ by trace preservation. Positivity and normalization of $J_B(\rho)/p(B)$ hold precisely when $p(B)>0$. Whether the prescribed instrument is experimentally realized remains a separate model assumption.

citations.quote: Assume AC. For a bounded self-adjoint operator $T$ on a nonzero complex Hilbert space there is a unique isometric unital star-homomorphism $C(\sigma(T))\to\mathcal B(H)$, $f\mapsto f(T)$, sending the coordinate function $z$ to $T$, with range $C^*(I,T)$.

Assume AC. Let $T$ be a bounded normal operator on a nonzero complex Hilbert
space $H$ and let $E$ be its spectral projection valued measure on the Borel
$\sigma$-algebra of $\sigma(T)$, the unique regular projection valued measure
with $\int z\,dE(z)=T$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-bounded-normal-operators-pvm-form]]). For a
**bounded Borel function** $f:\sigma(T)\to\mathbb C$, that is a bounded
$\Sigma$-measurable function on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\sigma(T)$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]), define the **Borel
functional calculus** of $T$ at $f$ by

$$f(T):=\Phi_E(f)=\int_{\sigma(T)}f\,dE,$$

the bounded Borel integral of $f$ against $E$ from
[[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]]. The map $f\mapsto f(T)$ from bounded Borel
functions on $\sigma(T)$ to $\mathcal B(H)$ is the **bounded Borel functional
calculus** of $T$.

**Well-definedness and consistency.** The operator $f(T)$ is well defined
because the spectral projection valued measure $E$ of $T$ is unique: if $E'$
were another regular projection valued measure with $\int z\,dE'=T$, then
$E'=E$. The construction agrees with the continuous calculus on continuous
functions, $\Phi_E(f)=f(T)$ for $f\in C(\sigma(T))$, by the displayed clause of
the spectral theorem. It inherits the algebraic behaviour of the projection
valued measure integral: $f(T)$ is complex-linear in $f$, unital with
$\mathbf 1(T)=I$, multiplicative, star-preserving with
$\overline f(T)=f(T)^*$, norm bounded by $\|f(T)\|\le\|f\|_\infty$, strongly
continuous for bounded Borel $f_n,f$ when $f_n\to f$ pointwise $E$-almost everywhere and
$\sup_n\|f_n\|_\infty<\infty$, as supplied by [[thm-pvm-integral-is-a-star-homomorphism]]. In particular
$\mathbf 1_B(T)=E(B)$ for every Borel set $B\subseteq\sigma(T)$, and the norm of
$f(T)$ is the $E$-essential supremum of $f$
([[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]]).


**Commutation.** Every bounded $S$ commuting with $T$ and $T^*$ commutes
with every $f(T)$.  Write $\pi(g)=g(T)$ for the continuous calculus. The
construction in [[lem-continuous-functional-calculus-produces-a-regular-pvm]]
provides finite regular complex measures $\mu_{x,y}$ with
$\mu_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ and
$\int g\,d\mu_{x,y}=\langle\pi(g)x,y\rangle$ for continuous $g$; its PVM
is the present $E$ by uniqueness. The continuous commutant property
([[thm-continuous-functional-calculus-properties]]) and the defining adjoint
identity ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]) give
$$\int g\,d\mu_{Sx,y}=\langle\pi(g)Sx,y\rangle=\langle S\pi(g)x,y\rangle=\langle\pi(g)x,S^*y\rangle=\int g\,d\mu_{x,S^*y}.$$
Uniqueness of the finite regular complex representing measure on the compact
spectrum, where $C_0(\sigma(T))=C(\sigma(T))$, gives
$\mu_{Sx,y}=\mu_{x,S^*y}$
([[thm-bounded-c-zero-functionals-are-regular-complex-measure-integrals]]).
For bounded Borel $f$, the bounded-integral pairing identity therefore yields
$$\langle f(T)Sx,y\rangle=\int f\,d\mu_{Sx,y}=\int f\,d\mu_{x,S^*y}=\langle Sf(T)x,y\rangle.$$
Testing the difference against itself proves $f(T)S=Sf(T)$. These properties are collected in
[[thm-borel-functional-calculus-for-bounded-normal-operators]].

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space of dimension $d\ge1$ ([[def-hilbert-space]]), with adjoints as in [[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]] and the finite trace as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Recall that an endomorphism $F$ is an **effect** when $F\ge0$ and $I-F\ge0$, i.e. $0\le F\le I$ in the quadratic-form order ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]).

(a) *Definitions.* A finite POVM is a finite family $(F_a)_{a=1}^p$ of effects with $\sum_aF_a=I$. An **instrument** is a finite family $(M_{a,r})_{a,r}$ of endomorphisms of $H$; its outcome effects and updates are $F_a:=\sum_rM_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}$ and $I_a(R):=\sum_rM_{a,r}RM_{a,r}^*$. It is **normalized** when $\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I$.

(b) If $(F_a)$ is a finite POVM and $\rho$ a density operator ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]) then $p_a:=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)\ge0$ and $\sum_ap_a=1$. If $(M_{a,r})$ is a normalized instrument then the $F_a$ form a finite POVM, $\operatorname{tr}I_a(\rho)=p_a$, each $I_a(\rho)$ is non-negative, and whenever $p_a>0$ the normalized update $I_a(\rho)/p_a$ is a density operator.

(c) *Ideal Lüders case.* For an orthogonal projection $P$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]) put $M_0=P$, $M_1=I-P$. Then $\sum_jM_j^*M_j=P+(I-P)=I$, the effects are $F_0=P$, $F_1=I-P$, and $I_j(\rho)=P\rho P$ or $(I-P)\rho(I-P)$.

[Outcome projections] By [F2] each $P_a=\sum_rI\otimes T_{e_{a,r},e_{a,r}}$ is the orthogonal projection onto $H\widehat\otimes\overline{\operatorname{span}}\{e_{a,r}:r\ge1\}$, the strong sums over $a$ telescope to $I$, and $P_aP_b=\delta_{ab}P_a$.

[Compression] As in the finite case, $W^*(\xi\otimes e_{a,r})=M_{a,r}^*\xi$ because $W$ is an isometry with the displayed action, so $W^*P_aW\psi=\sum_rM_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}\psi$ for every $\psi$, the strong limit defining $F_a$.

[Partial-trace recovery by truncations] For $x,y\in H$ and a finite rectangle $D$ of index pairs put $w_D:=\sum_{(a,r)\in D}M_{a,r}x\otimes e_{a,r}$ and $z_D:=\sum_{(a,r)\in D}M_{a,r}y\otimes e_{a,r}$. Both sides are bounded linear maps on trace class: the left side by the two-sided ideal bound for $W,W^*$ and [F3], and the right side by nuclear expansion and the preceding rank-one bound. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
