Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

If $f:\Omega\to X$ is Bochner integrable, then for every measurable $E$,

$$\left\|\int_E f\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|f\|\,d\mu.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $f_n:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable,
suppose $f_n(\omega)\to f(\omega)$ in norm for almost every $\omega$, and let
$g$ be a nonnegative integrable scalar function with
$\|f_n(\omega)\|\leq g(\omega)$ almost everywhere for every $n$. Then $f$ and
all $f_n$ are Bochner integrable,

$$\int\|f_n-f\|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$

and $\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu$ in norm.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,K$ be nonzero complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $H\widehat\otimes K$ be their completed tensor product ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]); write $T_{x,z}x'=\langle x',z\rangle x$ for rank-one operators ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]) and $\operatorname{tr}$ for the trace of a trace-class operator ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]).

(a) There is a unique linear map $\operatorname{Tr}_K:\mathcal S_1(H\widehat\otimes K)\to\mathcal S_1(H)$ with

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_KT)A\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(T(A\otimes I_K)\bigr)$$

for every trace-class $T$ and every $A\in\mathcal B(H)$; it satisfies $\|\operatorname{Tr}_KT\|_1\le\|T\|_1$ and is independent of any chosen orthonormal basis of $K$.

(b) $\operatorname{Tr}_K$ maps self-adjoint positive trace-class operators to self-adjoint positive trace-class operators (positivity in the bounded-operator sense of [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]), is trace preserving ($\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Tr}_KT=\operatorname{tr}T$), and maps density operators to density operators ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]).

(c) On rank-one operators, $\operatorname{Tr}_KT_{u\otimes v,u'\otimes v'}=\langle v,v'\rangle_K\,T_{u,u'}$.

The analogous map $\operatorname{Tr}_H$ satisfies $\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{Tr}_HT)A)=\operatorname{tr}(T(I_H\otimes A))$ for $A\in\mathcal B(K)$. No claim is made about instruments or conditioning.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and $K$
be Hilbert spaces over the same real or complex scalar field and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]). Then $T$ is trace class
([[def-trace-class-operator]]) if and only if there are families
$(u_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $H$ and $(v_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $K$, indexed by the positive
integers, with
$$\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<+\infty$$
such that the zero-based sequence of finite-rank operators defined by $R_0=0$
and
$$R_m:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\langle\cdot,u_j\rangle v_j\qquad(m\ge1)$$
converges to $T$ in operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]],
[[def-metric-convergence]]).  Here the displayed scalar series is, under the
library convention, the series of the sequence
$(\|u_{m+1}\|\,\|v_{m+1}\|)_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case
$$\|T\|_1=\inf\Bigl\{\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|:\ R_m\to T\ \text{in operator norm}\Bigr\},$$
the infimum being over all such **nuclear representations** of $T$, with the
same zero-based shift understood in every displayed sum, and the
infimum is attained: using its positive-integer index set and padding finite rank by zeros,
the singular-value series
$T=\sum_{j\in J}s_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ is a nuclear representation with
sum $\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

In a measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ ([[def-measure-space]]), a measurable set $N\in\mathcal A$ is **$\mu$-null** if $\mu(N)=0$.

A property $P(x)$ holds **$\mu$-almost everywhere**, or **for $\mu$-almost every $x$**, if its exceptional set is contained in a measurable $\mu$-null set: there is $N\in\mathcal A$ with $\mu(N)=0$ such that $P(x)$ holds for every $x\in X\setminus N$. Both notions are relative to the named measure $\mu$.

derivations.claim: [Construction and completeness of the Hilbert target] Coordinate Cauchy–Schwarz makes the inner product of $E=\ell^2(H)$ absolutely convergent and gives its squared norm $\sum_r\|z_r\|^2$. If $(z^{(n)})$ is Cauchy in this norm, each coordinate converges in the complete space $H$ to $z_r$; taking limits of finite squared sums shows $\sum_r\|z_r\|^2<\infty$ and $\|z^{(n)}-z\|_E\to0$. Thus $E$ is Hilbert. Strongly measurable $E$-valued fields have measurable norm and inner-product functions by their simple approximants; scalar Cauchy–Schwarz [F6] gives absolute integrability of the target inner product. This integral descends to the almost-everywhere quotient, is positive definite there, and has the stated norm; scalar Minkowski gives its triangle inequality. For completeness, take a Cauchy sequence of classes and a subsequence with representatives $f_k$ satisfying $\|f_{k+1}-f_k\|_2\le2^{-k}$; Countable Choice permits the countable representative selection. Set $d_k=f_{k+1}-f_k$. For $g_N:=\sum_{k\le N}\|d_k(\cdot)\|_E$, scalar Minkowski gives $\|g_N\|_2\le\sum_{k\le N}2^{-k}\le1$. Monotone convergence [F6] applied to $g_N^2$ gives $g:=\sum_k\|d_k\|_E\in L^2$ and $g<\infty$ almost everywhere. Hence $f_1+\sum_kd_k$ converges pointwise off a measurable null set in complete $E$; define its limit as zero on that set. The limit is strongly measurable: the countably many simple approximant ranges for all $f_k$ have a separable closed span, norm distances to a countable dense subset are measurable, and choosing the nearest of the first $N$ dense points gives finite-valued simple approximants converging pointwise. Scalar Minkowski and monotone convergence also give $\|f-f_k\|_2\le\sum_{j\ge k}2^{-j}\to0$, and $f\in L^2$ since $\|f\|_E\le\|f_1\|_E+g$. The original Cauchy sequence converges to the same class by the triangle inequality. Therefore the defined target is a Hilbert space; the construction uses no assumption that $\mu(X)$ is finite.

[The $L^2$ isometry] Fix $\psi\in H$. The measurable nonnegative function $g_\psi(x):=\sum_r\|M_r(x)\psi\|^2$ has finite integral $\|\psi\|^2$, so it is finite outside a null set. On that set the finite coordinate truncations converge in $\ell^2(H)$; define the vector field to be zero on the exceptional null set. The truncations are strongly measurable and their pointwise limit is strongly measurable, as follows directly by approximation with simple functions (or by separability of $\ell^2(H)$ and measurable coordinates). The field belongs to $L^2(X;\ell^2(H))$ because its squared norm is $g_\psi$ almost everywhere. Its equivalence class defines $W\psi$, independently of the null-set representative. For any finite collection of vectors, the coordinate linear identities hold outside the union of their exceptional sets, so $W$ is linear as a map of equivalence classes; normalization gives $\|W\psi\|=\|\psi\|$, hence $W$ is a linear isometry. No $L^1$ integrability of this raw vector field is needed.

[The PVM and the effects] Multiplication by $\mathbf1_B$ on $L^2$ is a bounded self-adjoint projection, with $P(X)=I$ and $P(B\cap C)=P(B)P(C)$. For disjoint $B_j$ with union $B$, put $U_N=\bigcup_{j\le N}B_j$. The squared $L^2$ norm of $(P(B)-\sum_{j\le N}P(B_j))f$ is $\int_{B\setminus U_N}\|f(x)\|^2d\mu$; this tends to zero because $\mathbf1_{U_N}\|f\|^2\uparrow\mathbf1_B\|f\|^2$ and monotone convergence applies. Thus $P$ is a PVM. Compression gives self-adjoint positive contractions $F(B)=W^*P(B)W$, normalization $F(X)=I$, and weak countable additivity. Equivalently, for every $u,v$, $\langle F(B)u,v\rangle=\int_B\sum_r\langle M_r(x)u,M_r(x)v\rangle\,d\mu$, with absolute convergence by Cauchy–Schwarz and normalization. This is the normalized POVM asserted in (b).

[Integrable cross fields] For $u,v\in H$, each $x\mapsto T_{M_r(x)u,M_r(x)v}$ is strongly measurable in trace norm by [F2]. By Cauchy–Schwarz twice and normalization, $$\int_X\sum_r\|M_r(x)u\|\,\|M_r(x)v\|\,d\mu\le\|u\|\,\|v\|.$$ Thus, outside a null set, the rank-one series converges absolutely in trace norm. Its sum $K_{u,v}(x)$ is strongly measurable and Bochner integrable by [F3], with integrated norm at most $\|u\|\|v\|$. Define $E_B(u,v):=\int_BK_{u,v}(x)\,d\mu$. This is sesquilinear, satisfies $\|E_B(u,v)\|_1\le\|u\|\|v\|$, and has pairing $\operatorname{tr}(E_B(u,v)A)=\sum_r\int_B\langle A M_r(x)u,M_r(x)v\rangle d\mu$ for bounded $A$, by the boundedness of trace pairings and absolute integrability. In particular $E_B(u,u)$ is positive and $\operatorname{tr}E_B(u,u)=\langle F(B)u,u\rangle$.

[The bounded linear instrument] For a nuclear representation $T=\sum_jT_{u_j,v_j}$, define $I_B(T):=\sum_jE_B(u_j,v_j)$, converging in trace norm. The bound of step 4.1 gives $\|I_B(T)\|_1\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|$. This is independent of representation: for a nuclear representation of zero, Tonelli and step 4.1 allow exchanging its $j$ sum, the $r$ sum and each bounded-$A$ trace pairing with the integral. For each fixed $r,x$, the two-sided ideal bound makes $\sum_jM_r(x)T_{u_j,v_j}M_r(x)^*=M_r(x)0M_r(x)^*=0$ in trace norm. Therefore all the resulting pairings vanish; rank-one test operators and [F5] show the image is zero. The difference of two representations is such a zero representation, proving independence. Hence $I_B$ is linear, bounded with norm at most one by taking the nuclear infimum, and positive by positive spectral rank-one expansion. For positive $\rho=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ its definition is exactly the Bochner formula in (c), and absolute integrability gives the stated bounded-$A$ pairing. Taking $A=I$ gives $\operatorname{tr}I_B(T)=\operatorname{tr}(TF(B))$ first for rank-one inputs by step 3.1 and then for all inputs by nuclear continuity; in particular $I_X$ is trace preserving.

[Countable additivity and complete positivity] For disjoint $B_j$ with union $B$, the fields $\mathbf1_{U_N}K_{u,v}$, where $U_N=\bigcup_{j\le N}B_j$, converge pointwise almost everywhere to $\mathbf1_BK_{u,v}$ and are dominated in norm by the integrable function $\|K_{u,v}\|_1$; Bochner dominated convergence [F3] gives $E_B(u,v)=\sum_jE_{B_j}(u,v)$ in trace norm. For a nuclear input $T=\sum_kT_{u_k,v_k}$, [F2] and step 4.1 give In fact, $\sum_j\sum_k\|E_{B_j}(u_k,v_k)\|_1\le\sum_k\int_B\sum_r\|M_r(x)u_k\|\,\|M_r(x)v_k\|d\mu\le\sum_k\|u_k\|\,\|v_k\|<\infty$. Thus the two sums may be interchanged in trace norm, and the omitted event tails tend to zero; this proves countable additivity of $I_B(T)$ in trace norm. For each finite ancilla $\mathbb C^n$, act on $\mathbb C^n\widehat\otimes H$ with the pointwise Kraus maps $I\otimes M_r(x)$. For a vector $\xi=\sum_{k=1}^ne_k\otimes\xi_k$, the integrated squared output norm is $\sum_k\int_X\sum_r\|M_r(x)\xi_k\|^2d\mu=\|\xi\|^2$. The same construction as steps 4.1–5.1 therefore maps each self-adjoint positive rank-one $T_{\xi,\xi}$ to an integral of positive rank-one operators and extends positively to every self-adjoint positive trace-class amplified input. Expanding its finite ancilla matrix entries shows this extension equals the finite amplification of $I_B$. Thus every $I_B$ is completely positive, and together with additivity and trace preservation this establishes the full abstract instrument, not merely its restriction to positive inputs.

[Conditional updates] For a density operator $\rho$, $I_B(\rho)\ge0$ and $p(B)=\operatorname{tr}I_B(\rho)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F(B))$ by step 5.1. If $p(B)>0$, division gives a positive operator of trace one and hence the claimed density operator; if $p(B)=0$ no normalized update is defined. Nothing here claims a normalized singleton density or a universal representation theorem.

derivations.claim: [The reduced state] Expanding $T_{\Psi,\Psi}$ into its four rank-one summands and applying the rank-one rule [F2] termwise gives $\operatorname{Tr}_KT_{\Psi,\Psi}=|\alpha|^2T_{a,a}+|\beta|^2T_{b,b}+\alpha\overline\beta\langle e_1,e_2\rangle T_{a,b}+\overline\alpha\beta\langle e_2,e_1\rangle T_{b,a}$, which is (a). The trace-preserving partial trace [F2] gives $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\|\Psi\|^2$; expanding the tensor norm by [F1] gives the displayed normalization formula. Positivity follows from positivity of $T_{\Psi,\Psi}$ and the positive partial trace [F2], so trace one is exactly the density condition.

[The bin weight] By [F2], $\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_B)=|\alpha|^2\int_B|a|^2+|\beta|^2\int_B|b|^2+\alpha\overline\beta\langle e_1,e_2\rangle\int_Ba\overline b+\overline\alpha\beta\langle e_2,e_1\rangle\int_Bb\overline a$; since the last two integrals are conjugates of one another (because $\langle e_2,e_1\rangle=\overline{\langle e_1,e_2\rangle}$ and $\int_Bb\overline a=\overline{\int_Ba\overline b}$), their sum is $2\operatorname{Re}(\alpha\overline\beta\langle e_1,e_2\rangle\int_Ba\overline b)$, giving (b).

[The overlap bound] By [F3], $|\langle e_1,e_2\rangle|\le1$. Thus the modulus of the complex cross-term coefficient $\alpha\overline\beta\langle e_1,e_2\rangle$ is at most $|\alpha\beta|$, and the real cross-term contribution at $x$ is bounded in magnitude by $2|\alpha\beta|\,|a(x)b(x)|$. A complex phase may rotate that contribution, so no comparison of its real part with the real part for overlap one is asserted. When $e_1\perp e_2$, the overlap is zero and the cross term vanishes, leaving exactly the diagonal sum, as claimed in (c).

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and $\hbar>0$. Write $\mathcal F_2$ for the unitary Plancherel transform extending $\widehat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]); the $L^2$ spaces are Hilbert spaces by [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] and [[def-hilbert-space]]. For $\psi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, denote by $\widehat\psi$ the continuous representative of $\mathcal F_2\psi$ given by that absolutely convergent integral.

(a) For $\psi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ the momentum wavefunction

$$\psi_p(p):=(2\pi\hbar)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ip\cdot x/\hbar}\psi(x)\,dx$$

is well defined, bounded and continuous, and $\psi_p(p)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-d/2}\widehat\psi\bigl(p/(2\pi\hbar)\bigr)$ for every $p$; here $\widehat\psi$ is the stated continuous representative, not a point evaluation of an $L^2$ equivalence class.

(b) The dilation operator $D_\hbar g(p):=(2\pi\hbar)^{-d/2}g\bigl(p/(2\pi\hbar)\bigr)$ is a surjective linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ onto itself, with inverse $D_\hbar^{-1}g(\xi)=(2\pi\hbar)^{d/2}g(2\pi\hbar\,\xi)$.

(c) The formula $U_0\psi:=\psi_p$ defines a linear isometry $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)\to L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ (for the Lebesgue spaces $dx$ and $dp$) that extends uniquely to a surjective linear isometry $U:L^2(\mathbb R^d,dx)\to L^2(\mathbb R^d,dp)$; on Schwartz functions $U=D_\hbar\mathcal F_2$, and for every $\psi\in L^2(\mathbb R^d)$,

$$\|U\psi\|_{L^2(dp)}=\|\psi\|_{L^2(dx)} .$$

The normalization statement is: the substitution $\xi=p/(2\pi\hbar)$ carries $d\xi=(2\pi\hbar)^{-d}dp$, and the factor $(2\pi\hbar)^{-d/2}$ in $U_0$ is exactly what makes $U$ an isometry with respect to $dp$. No physical identification of $U\psi$ with a measured momentum distribution is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}z>0$ and $n\ge1$ let

$$G_n(z):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-z|x|^2}\,dx,$$

where $dx$ is product Lebesgue measure and the complex integral is computed from its real and imaginary parts. Equivalently, the absolutely convergent improper multiple integral used here is the cube-truncation limit $\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{[-R,R]^n}e^{-z|x|^2}\,dx$ of these finite Lebesgue integrals. For $n=1$ it also equals the sum of the two separately convergent one-sided improper Riemann integrals at $0$, computed componentwise ([[def-improper-integral-at-infinity]]); this agreement is proved below. Then:

(a) $G_n(z)$ converges absolutely for every $z$ with $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, and $G_1$ is holomorphic on the right half-plane $\Omega:=\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Re}z>0\}$ with $G_1'(z)=-\int_{\mathbb R}x^2e^{-zx^2}dx$ ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]], [[def-complex-domain]]);

(b) with $\operatorname{Log}$ the principal logarithm and the branch $z^{-1/2}:=\exp\bigl(-\tfrac12\operatorname{Log}z\bigr)$ on the slit plane ([[def-complex-logarithms-principal-logarithm-and-complex-powers]], [[cor-principal-logarithm-is-holomorphic-on-the-slit-plane]]),

$$G_1(z)=\sqrt{\pi}\,z^{-1/2},\qquad G_1(z)^2=\frac{\pi}{z}\qquad(z\in\Omega),$$

the value on the positive real axis being $G_1(t)=\sqrt{\pi/t}$ for $t>0$;

(c) for every $n\ge1$ and $z\in\Omega$, $G_n(z)=G_1(z)^n=(\pi/z)^{n/2}$, the power being the branch $(\pi/z)^{n/2}=\exp\bigl(\tfrac n2(\log\pi-\operatorname{Log}z)\bigr)$.

In particular the factor $(1+i\tau)^{-1/2}$ is defined by this branch for every real $\tau$, since $\operatorname{Re}(1+i\tau)=1>0$. No asymptotic or distributional interpretation is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$, whose completeness follows from [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] and whose Hilbert-space structure is defined in [[def-hilbert-space]].

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with
spectral projection valued measure $E$, and set
$U(t):=e^{itT}=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{it\lambda}\,dE(\lambda)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$.
Then $U$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group,
$U(t)D(T)=D(T)$ and $TU(t)=U(t)T$ on $D(T)$, and the derivative
$\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(U(t)x-x)$ exists exactly for $x\in D(T)$, where it equals
$iTx$. Thus the generator of $U$ is $G=iT$, with $D(G)=D(T)$.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) and let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Call $G : I \to \mathbb{R}$ a **primitive of $f$ on
$I$** when $G$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ as a function on $I$ with
$G' = f$ there ([[def-derivative]]). Then:

1. **Existence.** Fix $c_0 \in I$. The function
   $$F : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad F(x) \;:=\; \int_{c_0}^x f$$
   is defined at every $x \in I$ ([[def-oriented-integral]],
   [[def-the-integral-function]]) and is a primitive of $f$ on $I$.
2. **Uniqueness up to a constant.** If $G_1$ and $G_2$ are primitives of $f$ on
   $I$ then there is a real $k$ with $G_1(x) = G_2(x) + k$ for every $x \in I$.
3. **Evaluation.** If $a, b \in I$ with $a < b$ and $G$ is any primitive of $f$
   on $I$, then
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**The scope is exactly the continuous case, and that is not a limitation of the
proof.** An integrable function need not have a primitive, and a function with a
primitive need not be integrable; this corollary is precisely the intersection
where both fundamental theorems apply, and both witnesses are on the companion
page.

Let $f$ be Riemann integrable on every compact interval $[a,R]$ with $R>a$. The improper integral over the right-unbounded interval is
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx:=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_a^R f(x)\,dx,$$
provided this limit exists as a finite real number. In that case the improper integral **converges**; otherwise it diverges. In particular, a limit of $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ is divergence, not convergence to an extended-real value.

If $f$ is Riemann integrable on every $[R,b]$ with $R<b$, define
$$\int_{-\infty}^b f(x)\,dx:=\lim_{R\to-\infty}\int_R^b f(x)\,dx$$
under the same finite-limit convention. All finite integrals use the oriented convention.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: [The initial packet is a unit Schwartz vector] The derivative $\partial_x^k\psi_0$ equals $P_k(x)\psi_0(x)$ for a polynomial $P_k$: this follows by induction with the product rule [F6] applied to the three factors $(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/4}$, $e^{-(x-x_0)^2/(4\sigma^2)}$ and the bounded factor $e^{ip_0(x-x_0)/\hbar}$, each differentiation of the last factor multiplying it by the constant $ip_0/\hbar$. Since $x\mapsto x^jP_k(x)e^{-(x-x_0)^2/(4\sigma^2)}$ is bounded for all $j,k$ (the exponential decays faster than any polynomial), $\psi_0\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$ [F1]. By [F6] $\int_{\mathbb R}|\psi_0(x)|^2dx=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-y^2/(2\sigma^2)}dy=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}\sqrt\pi\,(2\sigma^2)^{1/2}=1$, using [F3] with $z=1/(2\sigma^2)$ and the substitution $x=x_0+y$.

[The complex shift identity] For $\operatorname{Re}a>0$ and $b\in\mathbb R$ one has $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-ay^2}e^{iby}dy=\sqrt{\pi/a}\,e^{-b^2/(4a)}$ with $\sqrt{\pi/a}:=\sqrt\pi\,a^{-1/2}$: setting $F(b):=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-ay^2+iby}dy$ (absolutely convergent since $|e^{-ay^2+iby}|=e^{-\operatorname{Re}(a)y^2}$ is integrable) and $G_R(b):=\int_{-R}^Re^{-ay^2+iby}dy$, the fundamental theorem and [F6] give $\frac{d}{db}G_R(b)=i\int_{-R}^Rye^{-ay^2+iby}dy$, and since $|y|e^{-\operatorname{Re}(a)y^2}$ is integrable, $G_R\to F$ pointwise with the difference quotients converging, so $F$ is differentiable with $F'(b)=i\int_{\mathbb R}ye^{-ay^2+iby}dy$; integrating $\partial_y(e^{-ay^2+iby})=(-2ay+ib)e^{-ay^2+iby}$ over $[-R,R]$ gives $\int_{-R}^R(-2ay+ib)e^{-ay^2+iby}dy=e^{-aR^2+ibR}-e^{-aR^2-ibR}$, of modulus at most $2e^{-\operatorname{Re}(a)R^2}\to0$, so [F6] as $R\to\infty$ gives $-2aF_y(b)+ibF(b)=0$ with $F_y(b):=\int_{\mathbb R}ye^{-ay^2+iby}dy$, hence $F_y=\frac{ib}{2a}F$ and $F'=-\frac{b}{2a}F$; the product rule [F6] gives $\frac{d}{db}[F(b)e^{b^2/(4a)}]=0$, so the product is constant (fundamental theorem applied to real and imaginary parts [F6]) and its value at $b=0$ is $F(0)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-ay^2}dy=\sqrt\pi\,a^{-1/2}$ by [F3].

[The free operator in momentum coordinates] Let $B$ be the multiplication operator $(B\varphi)(p)=\frac{p^2}{2m}\varphi(p)$ on $D(B):=\{\varphi\in L^2(dp):p^2\varphi\in L^2\}$; then $U^*BU=H_0$ with $D(H_0)=U^*D(B)$, and $H_0U^*=U^*B$, because $D_\hbar^*=D_\hbar^{-1}$ and $(D_\hbar^{-1}M_gD_\hbar h)(\xi)=g(2\pi\hbar\xi)h(\xi)$ for every Borel $g$ and every $h$ in the domain of $D_\hbar^{-1}M_gD_\hbar$, so with $g(p)=p^2/(2m)$ one has $U^*BU=\mathcal F_2^*D_\hbar^*M_{p^2/(2m)}D_\hbar\mathcal F_2=\mathcal F_2^*M_{2\pi^2\hbar^2\xi^2/m}\mathcal F_2=H_0$ as operators [F2, F4]; for the domains, $f\in D(H_0)$ means $\xi^2\mathcal F_2f\in L^2$, which by $Uf(p)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-1/2}\mathcal F_2f(p/(2\pi\hbar))$ is equivalent to $p^2Uf\in L^2$ (the substitution $\xi=p/(2\pi\hbar)$ and the constants $(2\pi\hbar)^{\pm2}$ preserve $L^2$-membership), i.e. to $Uf\in D(B)$, so $D(H_0)=U^*D(B)$, the identity $U^*BU=H_0$ holds on it, and multiplying on the right by $U^*$ gives $H_0U^*=U^*BUU^*=U^*B$.

[Fourier transform of the initial packet] Since $\psi_0\in L^1\cap L^2$ [step 1.1], $\mathcal F_2\psi_0$ is computed by the $L^1$ integral [F4]; substituting $x=x_0+y$ [F6] and using $\psi_0(x_0+y)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/4}e^{-y^2/(4\sigma^2)}e^{ip_0y/\hbar}$ gives $\mathcal F_2\psi_0(\xi)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/4}e^{-2\pi ix_0\xi}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-y^2/(4\sigma^2)}e^{i(p_0/\hbar-2\pi\xi)y}dy=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/4}e^{-2\pi ix_0\xi}2\sigma\sqrt\pi\,e^{-\sigma^2(p_0/\hbar-2\pi\xi)^2}$ by step 1.2 with $a=1/(4\sigma^2)$ and $b=p_0/\hbar-2\pi\xi$; since $\psi_0\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$, $U\psi_0=D_\hbar\mathcal F_2\psi_0$ [F2], so $\varphi_0:=U\psi_0$ satisfies $\varphi_0(p)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-1/2}\mathcal F_2\psi_0(p/(2\pi\hbar))=Ke^{-ix_0p/\hbar}e^{-\sigma^2(p-p_0)^2/\hbar^2}$ with $K:=(2\pi\hbar)^{-1/2}(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/4}2\sigma\sqrt\pi$ and $K^2=\sqrt{2/\pi}\,\sigma/\hbar$.

[The packet is Schwartz and its modulus is the spreading Gaussian] Putting $z_t:=1/(1+i\tau)$ (so $\operatorname{Re}z_t=1/(1+\tau^2)>0$) and $c_t:=x_0+p_0t/m$, one has $|\psi_t(x)|=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/4}|1+i\tau|^{-1/2}e^{-\operatorname{Re}(z_t)(x-c_t)^2/(4\sigma^2)}=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/4}(1+\tau^2)^{-1/4}e^{-(x-c_t)^2/(4\sigma^2(1+\tau^2))}$; the remaining $x$-dependent phase is $\exp(-i\operatorname{Im}(z_t)(x-c_t)^2/(4\sigma^2)+ip_0(x-x_0)/\hbar)$, which has modulus one. By the product rule, each $x$-derivative of $\psi_t$ is a polynomial in $x$ times $\psi_t$, so the displayed decaying modulus makes every polynomial-weighted derivative bounded and $\psi_t\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$; in particular $\psi_t\in L^1\cap L^2$ and $\psi_t\in D(H_0)$ by [F4].

[Momentum coordinates of the packet] With $A_t:=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/4}(1+i\tau)^{-1/2}$, $a_t:=1/(4\sigma^2(1+i\tau))$ and $b_\xi:=p_0/\hbar-2\pi\xi$, substituting $x=c_t+y$ [F6] in the $L^1$ integral [F4] of the packet $\psi_t=A_te^{-ip_0^2t/(2m\hbar)}e^{-a_t(x-c_t)^2}e^{i(p_0/\hbar)(x-x_0)}$ [step 2.2] gives $\mathcal F_2\psi_t(\xi)=A_t\sqrt{\pi/a_t}\,e^{ip_0^2t/(2m\hbar)}e^{-2\pi i\xi c_t}e^{-b_\xi^2/(4a_t)}$ by step 1.2 with $a=a_t$ (legal since $\operatorname{Re}a_t>0$); since $\psi_t\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$, $U\psi_t=D_\hbar\mathcal F_2\psi_t$ [F2], and with $p=2\pi\hbar\xi$, $\sqrt{\pi/a_t}=2\sigma\sqrt\pi(1+i\tau)^{1/2}$, $A_t(1+i\tau)^{1/2}=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/4}$ and $1/(4a_t)=\sigma^2(1+i\tau)$ one gets $U\psi_t(p)=Ke^{ip_0^2t/(2m\hbar)}e^{-ipc_t/\hbar}e^{-\sigma^2(p-p_0)^2/\hbar^2}e^{-it(p-p_0)^2/(2m\hbar)}$ with $K$ as in step 2.1.

[Position density, mean and variance] By step 2.2, $|\psi_t(x)|^2=(2\pi\sigma^2(1+\tau^2))^{-1/2}e^{-(x-c_t)^2/(2d_t^2)}$ with $c_t=x_0+p_0t/m$ and $d_t:=\sigma\sqrt{1+\tau^2}$; substituting $x=c_t+d_tu$ and using $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-u^2/2}du=\sqrt{2\pi}$ (that is [F3] with $z=1/2$) gives $\int_{\mathbb R}|\psi_t|^2=1$, while the centering $\int_{\mathbb R}(x-c_t)|\psi_t(x)|^2dx=d_t\int_{\mathbb R}u\frac{e^{-u^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}du=0$ and $\int_{\mathbb R}(x-c_t)^2|\psi_t(x)|^2dx=d_t^2\int_{\mathbb R}u^2\frac{e^{-u^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}du=d_t^2$, since $\int_{\mathbb R}u^2e^{-u^2/2}du=-G_1'(1/2)=\sqrt{2\pi}$ by [F3]; hence the density has mean $c_t=x_0+p_0t/m$ and variance $\sigma^2(1+\tau^2)$, which is clause (b).

[The packet is the free evolution of the momentum Gaussian] With $\theta_t(p):=tp^2/(2m\hbar)$ and $\varphi_t:=e^{-i\theta_t}\varphi_0$, steps 2.1 and 3.1 give $U\psi_t(p)=e^{-itp^2/(2m\hbar)}\varphi_0(p)=\varphi_t(p)$ for every $p$, because the two exponents differ by $i\bigl(p_0^2t/(2m\hbar)-p(x_0+p_0t/m)/\hbar-t(p-p_0)^2/(2m\hbar)+px_0/\hbar+tp^2/(2m\hbar)\bigr)=it\bigl(p_0^2-2pp_0-(p-p_0)^2+p^2\bigr)/(2m\hbar)=0$; hence $U\psi_t=\varphi_t$ and, $U$ being a surjective isometry [F2], $\psi_t=U^*\varphi_t$.

[Momentum density, mean and variance] By steps 2.1 and 3.1, $|U\psi_t(p)|^2=|\varphi_0(p)|^2=K^2e^{-2\sigma^2(p-p_0)^2/\hbar^2}=\sqrt{2/\pi}\frac{\sigma}{\hbar}e^{-(p-p_0)^2/(2w^2)}$ with $w:=\hbar/(2\sigma)$ and $K^2=\sqrt{2/\pi}\,\sigma/\hbar$; substituting $p=p_0+wu$ as in step 3.2 gives total mass $1$, mean $p_0$ and variance $w^2=\hbar^2/(4\sigma^2)$, and the density does not depend on $t$; this is clause (c).

[The momentum path solves the momentum equation] Put $q(p):=p^2/(2m\hbar)$ and $\varphi_t(p):=e^{-itq(p)}\varphi_0(p)$. The Gaussian formula of step 2.1 gives $q\varphi_0\in L^2(dp)$ and $p^2\varphi_0\in L^2(dp)$, so $\varphi_t\in D(B)$ for every $t$. For fixed $t$ and $h\ne0$, $\frac{\varphi_{t+h}(p)-\varphi_t(p)}h=\varphi_t(p)\frac{e^{-ihq(p)}-1}h$ tends pointwise to $-iq(p)\varphi_t(p)=-(i/\hbar)\frac{p^2}{2m}\varphi_t(p)$. Since $|e^{-is}-1|\le|s|$, the difference between the quotient and its limit has squared modulus at most $4|q(p)\varphi_0(p)|^2$, an integrable function; dominated convergence [F6] therefore gives convergence in $L^2(dp)$. Also $\varphi_{t+h}\to\varphi_t$ and $B\varphi_{t+h}\to B\varphi_t$ in $L^2(dp)$ by pointwise convergence and the respective integrable square majorants $4|\varphi_0|^2$ and $4|B\varphi_0|^2$. Thus $t\mapsto\varphi_t$ is continuously differentiable with $\varphi_t'=-(i/\hbar)B\varphi_t$. Consequently $\psi_t=U^*\varphi_t$ [step 4.1] is $C^1$ in $L^2$, lies in $D(H_0)=U^*D(B)$, and $\frac{d}{dt}\psi_t=U^*\varphi_t'= -\frac{i}{\hbar}U^*B\varphi_t=-\frac{i}{\hbar}H_0U^*\varphi_t=-\frac{i}{\hbar}H_0\psi_t$, using that $U^*$ is an isometry [F2] and $H_0U^*=U^*B$ from step 1.3; at $t=0$ the formula of the Statement reduces to $\psi_0$.

[Uniqueness of the Cauchy problem] Let $V(t):=e^{itT}$ with $T:=-H_0/\hbar$ [F5]; since $\psi_0\in D(H_0)=D(T)$ [step 1.1, F4], one has $V(t)\psi_0\in D(T)$ for all $t$ and $t\mapsto V(t)\psi_0$ is $C^1$ with $\frac{d}{dt}V(t)\psi_0=iTV(t)\psi_0=-\frac{i}{\hbar}H_0V(t)\psi_0$, because [F5] gives $\frac1h(V(t+h)-V(t))\psi_0=V(t)\frac1h(V(h)\psi_0-\psi_0)\to V(t)(iT\psi_0)$ as $\psi_0\in D(T)$ and $V(t)$ is bounded, and $TV(t)=V(t)T$ on $D(T)$ by [F5]; by step 5.1, $w_t:=\psi_t-V(t)\psi_0$ is $C^1$ with $w_t\in D(H_0)$ and $w_t'=-\frac{i}{\hbar}H_0w_t$, and $w_0=0$ since $V(0)=I$ and the Statement's formula at $t=0$ is the initial packet; for the real function $t\mapsto\|w_t\|^2$ one has $\frac{\|w_{t+h}\|^2-\|w_t\|^2}{h}=2\operatorname{Re}\langle w_t,\frac{w_{t+h}-w_t}{h}\rangle+\frac{\|w_{t+h}-w_t\|^2}{h}\to2\operatorname{Re}\langle w_t,w_t'\rangle$, the last term tending to $0$; now, since the inner product is conjugate-linear in its second argument, $\langle w_t,w_t'\rangle=\langle w_t,-\frac{i}{\hbar}H_0w_t\rangle=\frac{i}{\hbar}\langle w_t,H_0w_t\rangle$. The number $\langle w_t,H_0w_t\rangle=\langle H_0w_t,w_t\rangle$ is real because $H_0$ is self-adjoint, hence symmetric, on $D(H_0)$ [F4], so $\operatorname{Re}\langle w_t,w_t'\rangle=0$ and $\|w_t\|^2$ has vanishing derivative, hence is constant by the fundamental theorem [F6] and equals $\|w_0\|^2=0$; thus $\psi_t=V(t)\psi_0=e^{-itH_0/\hbar}\psi_0$ for every $t$, which is clause (a).

[Operator standard deviations] For $\psi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$ one has $U(P\psi)=M_pU\psi$ with $(M_pg)(p)=pg(p)$, because $\mathcal F_2(P\psi)(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R}(-i\hbar\psi'(x))e^{-2\pi ix\xi}dx=2\pi\hbar\xi\,\mathcal F_2\psi(\xi)$ by integration by parts, the boundary terms $[\psi(x)e^{-2\pi ix\xi}]$ vanishing at $\pm\infty$ as $\psi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$ [F6], and applying $D_\hbar$ with $p=2\pi\hbar\xi$ gives the claim [F2]; the unit vector $\psi_t$ of step 6.1 is the packet of steps 3.2 and 4.2, and for it this gives $b_t:=\langle P\psi_t,\psi_t\rangle=\langle UP\psi_t,U\psi_t\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}p|U\psi_t(p)|^2dp=p_0$, a real number, and $\Delta P:=\|(P-b_t)\psi_t\|_2=\|U(P-b_t)\psi_t\|_2=\bigl(\int_{\mathbb R}(p-p_0)^2|U\psi_t(p)|^2dp\bigr)^{1/2}=\hbar/(2\sigma)$ by step 4.2, while $a_t:=\langle Q\psi_t,\psi_t\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}x|\psi_t(x)|^2dx=c_t$ and $\Delta Q:=\|(Q-a_t)\psi_t\|_2=\bigl(\int_{\mathbb R}(x-c_t)^2|\psi_t(x)|^2dx\bigr)^{1/2}=\sigma\sqrt{1+\tau^2}$ by step 3.2; hence $\Delta Q\Delta P=\frac{\hbar}{2}\sqrt{1+\tau^2}$.

[Robertson comparison and scope] By [F7] with $c=\hbar$, applied to the unit Schwartz vector $\psi_t$ of step 7.1, one has $\Delta Q\Delta P\ge\hbar/2$; the exact value of step 7.1 is $\frac{\hbar}{2}\sqrt{1+\tau^2}$, which equals $\hbar/2$ exactly when $\tau=0$, i.e. exactly at $t=0$ since $\tau=\hbar t/(2m\sigma^2)$, and is strictly larger otherwise; thus clause (d) holds, and clause (e) records that all of the above are computations inside the free model defined by $H_0$, with no measurement interpretation.

boundaries.reason: No empty index set or empty domain is quantified over: the Statement fixes $m,\hbar,\sigma>0$, $x_0,p_0\in\mathbb R$, the vector $\psi_0$ above, the operator $H_0$ and the transform $U$..

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). By the orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]) every $x\in H$ has a unique representation

$$x=P_Mx+(x-P_Mx),\qquad P_Mx\in M,\quad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp ,$$

and the **Hilbert orthogonal projection onto $M$** is the map

$$P_M:H\longrightarrow M\subseteq H,\qquad x\longmapsto P_Mx ,$$

assigning to $x$ its unique $M$-component. Its defining properties are therefore

$$P_Mx\in M,\qquad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp\qquad(x\in H),$$

which characterise $P_M$ uniquely: a map with these defining properties must agree with the $M$-component of the unique decomposition of each $x$.

**Agreement with the finite-dimensional projection.** If $V$ is a finite-dimensional inner-product space and $W\subseteq V$ a subspace, then [[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]] writes $V=W\oplus W^\perp$ and [[def-orthogonal-projection]] defines $P_Wv$ as the unique $W$-component of $v$; the defining properties displayed above are the same, so they define the same map on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.

**Range and kernel.** $P_Mx\in M$ for every $x$, and $P_Mm=m$ for $m\in M$ because $m=m+0$ with $0\in M^\perp$; conversely $P_Mx=0$ says exactly that $x=x-0\in M^\perp$. Hence the range of $P_M$ is $M$ and its kernel is $M^\perp$, and $P_M$ is the identity on $M$ and zero on $M^\perp$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$,
and for $x,y\in H$ define

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad E_{x,y}(B):=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle \qquad(B\in\Sigma).$$

Then:

1. $E_x$ is a positive measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ with $E_x(X)=\|x\|^2$ and
   $0\le E_x(B)\le\|x\|^2$ for every $B$;
2. $E_{x,y}$ is a finite complex measure on $(X,\Sigma)$, the map
   $(x,y)\mapsto E_{x,y}$ is linear in $x$ and conjugate-linear in $y$, and
   $E_{y,x}=\overline{E_{x,y}}$, meaning $E_{y,x}(B)=\overline{E_{x,y}(B)}$ for
   every $B$;
3. $|E_{x,y}|(X)\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$, so $|E_{x,y}(B)|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$ for every
   $B$, and the polarization identity
   $$E_{x,y}=\frac14\sum_{k=0}^{3}i^kE_{x+i^ky}$$
   holds as an identity of complex measures, where $i^k$ are the fourth roots
   of unity $1,i,-1,-i$.

Let $\mathcal A_0$ be an algebra of subsets of $X$. A **premeasure** on an algebra $\mathcal A_0$ vanishes at the empty set and is countably additive whenever a disjoint sequence in $\mathcal A_0$ has its union in $\mathcal A_0$. Thus $\mu_0:\mathcal A_0\to[0,+\infty]$ is a premeasure when $\mu_0(\varnothing)=0$ and

$$\mu_0\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}A_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu_0(A_k)$$

whenever the $A_k$ are pairwise disjoint members of $\mathcal A_0$ and their union belongs to $\mathcal A_0$. Padding a finite disjoint family by empty sets shows that a premeasure is finitely additive.

The premeasure is **finite** if $\mu_0(X)<+\infty$. It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal A_0$ with $X=\bigcup_nP_n$ and $\mu_0(P_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The outer set function induced by a premeasure is an outer measure.
For an outer measure $\mu^*$ on $X$, the Carathéodory measurable subsets form a sigma-algebra, and the restriction of the outer measure to it is a complete measure.
For every $A\in\mathcal A_0$, the outer measure induced by a premeasure satisfies $\mu^*(A)=\mu_0(A)$.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every member of the source algebra is Carathéodory measurable for the induced outer measure.
A finite premeasure has at most one measure extension to the sigma-algebra generated by its source algebra.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $X$ be a set. A **pi-system on $X$** is a nonempty family
$\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ closed under binary intersections: if
$A,B\in\mathcal P$, then $A\cap B\in\mathcal P$.

The nonempty-family requirement is the convention used here. It does not require
$X\in\mathcal P$ and it does not add an empty-intersection axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $X$ be LCH and suppose every open subset of $X$ is sigma-compact. Every Borel measure finite on compact sets is regular: it is outer regular on Borel sets and inner regular by compact sets on every Borel set.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

derivations.claim: [The finitely additive projection on the rectangle algebra] For a finite disjoint union $A=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^n(B_i\times C_i)$ of measurable rectangles put $P(A):=\sum_iE(B_i)F(C_i)$. This is well defined: two finite rectangle decompositions have a common refinement into disjoint rectangles (intersections of the pieces), and on a common refinement both sums agree by additivity of $E$ and $F$; in particular $P(\varnothing)=0$ and $P(\mathbb R^2)=I$. Each $E(B_i)F(C_i)$ is an orthogonal projection because $(E(B_i)F(C_i))^2=E(B_i)^2F(C_i)^2=E(B_i)F(C_i)$ and $(E(B_i)F(C_i))^*=F(C_i)E(B_i)=E(B_i)F(C_i)$ by [F1] and strong commutation; summands belonging to disjoint rectangles are orthogonal, since $E(B_i)F(C_i)E(B_j)F(C_j)=E(B_i\cap B_j)F(C_i\cap C_j)=0$. Hence $P(A)$ is a sum of pairwise orthogonal projections, so $P(A)^2=P(A)=P(A)^*$; and from the refinement description $P$ is finitely additive on disjoint unions, $P(A\cap A')=P(A)P(A')$ and $P(A\cup A')=P(A)+P(A')$ for disjoint $A,A'\in\mathcal A_0$.

[Uniqueness for finite complex measures] Let $\mu,
u$ be finite complex measures on $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)$ that agree on $\mathcal A_0$, which contains $\mathbb R^2$. Then $\mathcal D:=\{S\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2):\mu(S)=
u(S)\}$ contains $\mathbb R^2$ and the $\pi$-system $\mathcal A_0$; it is a $\lambda$-system because equality on the whole space gives closure under complements and countable additivity gives closure under disjoint countable unions. By Dynkin's $\pi$-$\lambda$ theorem [F8], $\mathcal D$ contains $\sigma(\mathcal A_0)=\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)$ by [F5], so $\mu=
u$ on every Borel set.

[The scalar set functions are premeasures] For $\psi\in H$ define $\mu_\psi(A):=\langle P(A)\psi,\psi\rangle=\|P(A)\psi\|^2$ for $A\in\mathcal A_0$; by step 1.1, $\mu_\psi(\varnothing)=0$, $\mu_\psi$ is finitely additive, and $\mu_\psi\le\|\psi\|^2$. To verify countable additivity, fix pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal A_0$ with union $A\in\mathcal A_0$ and put $R_N:=A\setminus\bigcup_{n\le N}A_n\in\mathcal A_0$. Finite additivity gives $\mu_\psi(A)=\sum_{n\le N}\mu_\psi(A_n)+\mu_\psi(R_N)$, and $R_N\downarrow\varnothing$, so continuity from above at $\varnothing$ implies $\mu_\psi(A)=\sum_n\mu_\psi(A_n)$. It remains to prove that continuity: for $A_n\downarrow\varnothing$ in $\mathcal A_0$, show $\mu_\psi(A_n)\to0$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, approximate each $A_n$ from inside by a compact union of rectangles: for a rectangle $B\times C$ one has $P(B\times C)-P(K_B\times K_C)=E(B\setminus K_B)F(C)+E(K_B)F(C\setminus K_C)$ with the two summands orthogonal, so $\mu_\psi(B\times C)-\mu_\psi(K_B\times K_C)\le E_\psi(B\setminus K_B)+F_\psi(C\setminus K_C)$ for $E_\psi(B)=\langle E(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$, $F_\psi(C)=\langle F(C)\psi,\psi\rangle$; by regularity [F1] compact $K_B\subseteq B$, $K_C\subseteq C$ make this arbitrarily small, and finite unions are handled by summing. Choose compact $L_n\subseteq A_n$ with $\mu_\psi(A_n\setminus L_n)<\varepsilon2^{-n}$. If $\mu_\psi(A_n)\ge\varepsilon$ for all $n$, then for every $N$ additivity and $L_1\cap\dots\cap L_N\supseteq A_N\setminus\bigcup_{n\le N}(A_n\setminus L_n)$ give $\mu_\psi(L_1\cap\dots\cap L_N)\ge\mu_\psi(A_N)-\sum_{n\le N}\mu_\psi(A_n\setminus L_n)\ge\varepsilon-\sum_{n\le N}\varepsilon2^{-n}>0$; hence every finite intersection $L_1\cap\dots\cap L_N$ is nonempty, and compactness gives a point of $\bigcap_nL_n\subseteq\bigcap_nA_n=\varnothing$, a contradiction. Thus $\mu_\psi(A_n)\to0$, and $\mu_\psi$ is a finite premeasure on $\mathcal A_0$.

[Carathéodory extension and polarization] By steps 1.1 and 2.1 the algebra $\mathcal A_0$ of finite unions of measurable rectangles is a $\pi$-system containing $\mathbb R^2$ and generates $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)$ by [F5]; hence $\mu_\psi$ extends to a finite measure $
u_\psi$ on $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)$, unique by [F3], and $
u_\psi(S)=\mu_\psi(S)$ for $S\in\mathcal A_0$. Uniqueness also extends the scalar homogeneity $
u_{\alpha x}=|\alpha|^2
u_x$ and the parallelogram identity from $\mathcal A_0$ to every Borel set: the corresponding finite positive measures agree on $\mathcal A_0$ and have the same total mass. For $x,y\in H$ define $
u_{x,y}(S):= rac14\sum_{k=0}^3i^k
u_{x+i^ky}(S)$; this is a finite complex measure and for $S\in\mathcal A_0$ it coincides with $\langle P(S)x,yangle$ by the polarization identity [F2]. The scalar homogeneity and parallelogram identity imply, by expansion of the four polarization terms, that $(x,y)\mapsto
u_{x,y}(S)$ is sesquilinear and Hermitian for every Borel $S$, with $
u_{x,x}(S)=
u_x(S)\ge0$. Positivity gives Cauchy–Schwarz for this form (apply $0\le
u_{x+\lambda y}(S)$ for all $\lambda\in\mathbb C$), so $|
u_{x,y}(S)|\le
u_x(S)^{1/2}
u_y(S)^{1/2}\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$.

[Multiplicativity and the PVM axioms] First observe that for arbitrary Borel $S$ and rectangle $R=B'	imes C'$, for every $x,y$ the scalar set functions $S'\mapsto\langle G(S'\cap R)x,yangle=
u_{x,y}(S'\cap R)$ and $S'\mapsto\langle G(S')G(R)x,yangle=
u_{G(R)x,y}(S')$ are finite complex measures; they agree on rectangles $S'=B	imes C$ because $G(S'\cap R)=E(B\cap B')F(C\cap C')=E(B)E(B')F(C)F(C')=E(B)F(C)E(B')F(C')=G(S')G(R)$ by [F1] and the commutation hypothesis, and they agree on $\mathbb R^2$ since each value is $G(R)$. u_{x,G(S)y}(T)$; by the previous result they agree on every rectangle $T$, and by step 1.2 [F8] they agree for all Borel $T$. Taking $S=T$ yields $G(S)^2=G(S)$, so every $G(S)$ is an orthogonal projection; $G(\varnothing)=0$ and $G(\mathbb R^2)=I$ follow from the rectangle values. u_x(S_n)$, so $\sum_n\|G(S_n)x\|^2=\sum_n
u_{x}(S_n)=
u_x(S)\le\|x\|^2<\infty$ and the orthogonal series $\sum_nG(S_n)x$ converges in norm to a vector whose pairings with every $y$ equal $\sum_n

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). By the orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]) every $x\in H$ has a unique representation

$$x=P_Mx+(x-P_Mx),\qquad P_Mx\in M,\quad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp ,$$

and the **Hilbert orthogonal projection onto $M$** is the map

$$P_M:H\longrightarrow M\subseteq H,\qquad x\longmapsto P_Mx ,$$

assigning to $x$ its unique $M$-component. Its defining properties are therefore

$$P_Mx\in M,\qquad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp\qquad(x\in H),$$

which characterise $P_M$ uniquely: a map with these defining properties must agree with the $M$-component of the unique decomposition of each $x$.

**Agreement with the finite-dimensional projection.** If $V$ is a finite-dimensional inner-product space and $W\subseteq V$ a subspace, then [[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]] writes $V=W\oplus W^\perp$ and [[def-orthogonal-projection]] defines $P_Wv$ as the unique $W$-component of $v$; the defining properties displayed above are the same, so they define the same map on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.

**Range and kernel.** $P_Mx\in M$ for every $x$, and $P_Mm=m$ for $m\in M$ because $m=m+0$ with $0\in M^\perp$; conversely $P_Mx=0$ says exactly that $x=x-0\in M^\perp$. Hence the range of $P_M$ is $M$ and its kernel is $M^\perp$, and $P_M$ is the identity on $M$ and zero on $M^\perp$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $E,F$ be **regular** projection-valued measures on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) satisfying the strong commutation relation

$$E(B)F(C)=F(C)E(B)\qquad\text{for all Borel }B,C\subseteq\mathbb R .$$

Then there is a unique regular projection-valued measure $G$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R^2$ with

$$G(B\times C)=E(B)F(C)\qquad\text{for every Borel rectangle }B\times C,$$

where rectangle means a measurable rectangle in the sense of [[def-measurable-rectangle]]. Its marginals are $G(B\times\mathbb R)=E(B)$ and $G(\mathbb R\times C)=F(C)$.

For the scalar construction, let $\mathcal A_0$ be the algebra of finite unions of Borel rectangles, and define $P_0(\bigsqcup_{i=1}^n B_i\times C_i):=\sum_{i=1}^nE(B_i)F(C_i)$ on disjoint rectangular decompositions. For every $\psi\in H$, $\mu_\psi(A):=\langle P_0(A)\psi,\psi\rangle$ is a finite premeasure on $\mathcal A_0$ and has a unique extension $G_\psi=\langle G(\cdot)\psi,\psi\rangle$ to the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. For $x,y\in H$, define the polarized measure $\nu_{x,y}:=\frac14\sum_{k=0}^3 i^kG_{x+i^ky}$. Then every Borel $S\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ has a unique bounded operator $G(S)$ satisfying $\langle G(S)x,y\rangle=\nu_{x,y}(S)$ for all $x,y\in H$, and $0\le G(S)\le I$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $E,F$ be **regular** projection-valued measures on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) satisfying the strong commutation relation

$$E(B)F(C)=F(C)E(B)\qquad\text{for all Borel }B,C\subseteq\mathbb R .$$

Then there is a unique regular projection-valued measure $G$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R^2$ with

$$G(B\times C)=E(B)F(C)\qquad\text{for every Borel rectangle }B\times C,$$

where rectangle means a measurable rectangle in the sense of [[def-measurable-rectangle]]. Its marginals are $G(B\times\mathbb R)=E(B)$ and $G(\mathbb R\times C)=F(C)$.

For the scalar construction, let $\mathcal A_0$ be the algebra of finite unions of Borel rectangles, and define $P_0(\bigsqcup_{i=1}^n B_i\times C_i):=\sum_{i=1}^nE(B_i)F(C_i)$ on disjoint rectangular decompositions. For every $\psi\in H$, $\mu_\psi(A):=\langle P_0(A)\psi,\psi\rangle$ is a finite premeasure on $\mathcal A_0$ and has a unique extension $G_\psi=\langle G(\cdot)\psi,\psi\rangle$ to the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. For $x,y\in H$, define the polarized measure $\nu_{x,y}:=\frac14\sum_{k=0}^3 i^kG_{x+i^ky}$. Then every Borel $S\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ has a unique bounded operator $G(S)$ satisfying $\langle G(S)x,y\rangle=\nu_{x,y}(S)$ for all $x,y\in H$, and $0\le G(S)\le I$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Here $|A|^{1/2}$ denotes the unbounded PVM integral $f(E_A)$ for $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{1/2}$, with domain $D(f(E_A))=\{\psi:\int |\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty\}$ as in [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and for $u,v\in H$ let $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) For every bounded $B\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]),

$$BT_{u,v}=T_{Bu,v},\qquad T_{u,v}B=T_{u,B^*v},$$

with the Hilbert adjoint $B^*$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class and let $T=\sum_jT_{u_j,v_j}$ be a nuclear representation, i.e. the partial sums converge to $T$ in operator norm and $\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<\infty$ ([[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then for every bounded $B$

$$\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\sum_j\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(TB)=\sum_j\langle u_j,B^*v_j\rangle,$$

both series converging absolutely with $\bigl|\operatorname{tr}(BT)\bigr|\le\|B\|\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|$, and $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). In particular $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ for every trace-class $T$ and bounded $B$, and $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\langle u,v\rangle$. No cyclic permutation of unbounded operators is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

derivations.claim: [Sharp bins and their products are projections] By [F1], $P_i=E(B_i)$ and $Q_j=F(C_j)$ are orthogonal projections; $P_iP_k=E(B_i)E(B_k)=E(B_i\cap B_k)=E(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne k$ and $Q_jQ_l=0$ for $j\ne l$; the commutation hypothesis and [F2] give $P_iQ_j=E(B_i)F(C_j)=G(B_i\times C_j)=F(C_j)E(B_i)=Q_jP_i$, so $R_{ij}=P_iQ_j=Q_jP_i$ is self-adjoint ($R_{ij}^*=Q_j^*P_i^*=Q_jP_i=R_{ij}$) and idempotent ($R_{ij}^2=P_iQ_jP_iQ_j=P_i(P_iQ_j)Q_j=P_i^2Q_j^2=P_iQ_j$), hence an orthogonal projection; also $R_{ij}R_{kl}=P_iQ_jP_kQ_l=P_iP_kQ_jQ_l$ using commutation, which vanishes unless $i=k$ and $j=l$.

[Trace and Born rules] For every bounded operator $B$ one has $\operatorname{tr}(\rho B)=\operatorname{tr}(B\rho)$, and $\operatorname{tr}(\rho\cdot)$ is linear in its bounded argument with $|\operatorname{tr}(\rho B)|\le\|B\|$; for every PVM and Borel set $S$ the number $\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(S))$ lies in $[0,1]$ and equals $\sum_nw_n\|E(S)u_n\|^2$ in any expansion of [F3], so $\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho G(B_i\times C_j))=\sum_nw_n\|G(B_i\times C_j)u_n\|^2$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_i)=\sum_nw_n\|P_iu_n\|^2$ are nonnegative and at most $1$.

[Sequential Lüders probability] If $\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_i)>0$, measuring the first instrument gives listed outcome $i$ with probability $\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_i)$ and state $\rho_i=P_i\rho P_i/\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_i)$ (stipulated, [F5]); measuring then the second gives conditional probability $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_iQ_j)=\operatorname{tr}(P_i\rho P_iQ_j)/\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_i)$. Cyclicity and $P_iQ_j=Q_jP_i$, $P_i^2=P_i$ give $\operatorname{tr}(P_i\rho P_iQ_j)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_iQ_jP_i)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_iQ_j)$, so the probability of the listed pair is $\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_iQ_j)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})$ by step 1.1. When $\operatorname{tr}(\rho Q_j)>0$, the reversed order gives conditional probability $\operatorname{tr}(Q_j\rho Q_jP_i)/\operatorname{tr}(\rho Q_j)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho Q_jP_i)/\operatorname{tr}(\rho Q_j)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})/\operatorname{tr}(\rho Q_j)$; multiplying by the probability of the first outcome gives the same joint probability. If a listed first outcome has zero probability, then $0\le R_{ij}\le P_i,Q_j$ and the positive density expansion [F3] give $\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})=0$, so the listed pair has probability zero and no division is taken.

[Order-independent conditional state] Assume $\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})>0$; running $(P_i)$ then $(Q_j)$ produces the product of the two stipulated denominator-normalizations, i.e. the state $Q_jP_i\rho P_iQ_j/\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})$ (by the computation of step 2.1), while the reversed order produces $P_iQ_j\rho Q_jP_i/\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})$; by step 1.1 both numerators equal $R_{ij}\rho R_{ij}$ and the denominators are the same positive number, so the two conditional states coincide and equal $R_{ij}\rho R_{ij}/\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})$, which is a density operator because $R_{ij}\rho R_{ij}$ is positive trace class with trace $\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})>0$ [F3, F4].

[Marginals of the joint law] If $\bigcup_jC_j=\mathbb R$, the finite additivity of a PVM gives $\sum_jQ_j=F(\bigcup_jC_j)=F(\mathbb R)=I$ [F1], so $\sum_j\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_iQ_j)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_i\sum_jQ_j)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_i)$ by linearity of $\operatorname{tr}(\rho\cdot)$ and the ideal property [F4]; symmetrically $\sum_i\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_iQ_j)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho Q_j)$ when $\bigcup_iB_i=\mathbb R$, so the joint law has the sharp-bin marginals.

[Repeatability] Let $\sigma:=R_{ij}\rho R_{ij}/\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})$ from step 3.1. Then $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma R_{ij})=\operatorname{tr}(R_{ij}\rho R_{ij}R_{ij})/\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})/\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})=1$ since $R_{ij}^2=R_{ij}$ and $R_{ij}R_{ij}R_{ij}=R_{ij}$ [step 1.1, F4]; likewise $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma P_i)=\operatorname{tr}(P_iR_{ij}\rho R_{ij}P_i)/\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})=\operatorname{tr}(R_{ij}\rho R_{ij})/\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})=1$ because $P_iR_{ij}=R_{ij}=R_{ij}P_i$, and $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma Q_j)=1$ the same way. Hence the Lüders updates $R_{ij}\sigma R_{ij}/\operatorname{tr}(\sigma R_{ij})$, $P_i\sigma P_i/\operatorname{tr}(\sigma P_i)$ and $Q_j\sigma Q_j/\operatorname{tr}(\sigma Q_j)$ all return the same state: e.g. $R_{ij}\sigma R_{ij}=R_{ij}^3\rho R_{ij}^3/\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})=R_{ij}\rho R_{ij}/\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})=\sigma$ and the denominators equal $1$, and similarly $P_i\sigma P_i=P_iR_{ij}\rho R_{ij}P_i/\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})=R_{ij}\rho R_{ij}/\operatorname{tr}(\rho R_{ij})=\sigma$ and $Q_j\sigma Q_j=\sigma$. Thus an immediate repetition of the pair, or of either single sharp measurement, returns the same outcome with probability $1$.

[Scope] Steps 2.1-4.1 are conditional computations inside the stipulated Lüders instrument and the joint PVM $G$ of [F2]; they assert joint probabilities, order independence and repeatability for that ideal model only, with no laboratory realization, no nonselective statement beyond step 3.2, and no time development.

Let $V,W$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner product spaces with orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_m)$ of $V$ and $(f_1,\dots,f_n)$ of $W$, let $V\otimes W$ be their tensor product with the inner product of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], and let $\operatorname{tr}$ denote the basis-independent trace of an endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

(a) For every endomorphism $R$ of $V\otimes W$ there is a unique endomorphism $\operatorname{Tr}_W R$ of $V$ with

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_WR)A\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R(A\otimes I_W)\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\operatorname{End}(V),$$

namely $\operatorname{Tr}_WR=\sum_{j=1}^n\varphi_j\circ R\circ\iota_j$, where $\iota_j(v)=v\otimes f_j$ and $\varphi_j(x\otimes w)=\langle w,f_j\rangle x$; it does not depend on the orthonormal basis $(f_j)$ of $W$, and the analogous definition gives $\operatorname{Tr}_V R$ with $\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{Tr}_VR)B)=\operatorname{tr}(R(I_V\otimes B))$.

(b) $\operatorname{Tr}_W$ is linear, positive (it maps positive endomorphisms to positive endomorphisms) and trace preserving on density matrices: if $R\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}R=1$ then $\operatorname{Tr}_WR\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Tr}_WR=1$; and $\operatorname{Tr}_W T_{\Psi,\Psi}=CC^*$ for every $\Psi\in V\otimes W$, where $C:W\to V$ is the coefficient map determined by $\Psi=\sum_jCf_j\otimes f_j$.

(c) *Schmidt decomposition.* Every $\Psi\in V\otimes W$ admits an expansion

$$\Psi=\sum_{r=1}^{k}s_r\,v_r\otimes u_r,$$

with $k\le\min(m,n)$, orthonormal families $(v_r)\subseteq V$, $(u_r)\subseteq W$ and $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_k>0$ uniquely determined by $\Psi$ as the positive singular values of the coefficient map; moreover $\|\Psi\|^2=\sum_rs_r^2$. For $\|\Psi\|=1$ the reduced density $\rho=\operatorname{Tr}_W T_{\Psi,\Psi}$ satisfies $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2=\sum_rs_r^4$, and $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2=1$ holds exactly when $k=1$, i.e. exactly when $\Psi$ is a product vector; mixed-state separability is not decided by this criterion.

(d) *Finite nonselective no-signalling.* If $(M_a)_{a=1}^p$ are endomorphisms of $W$ with $\sum_aM_a^*M_a=I_W$ then for every endomorphism $R$ of $V\otimes W$

$$\operatorname{Tr}_W\Bigl(\sum_a(I_V\otimes M_a)R(I_V\otimes M_a^*)\Bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}_WR .$$

This is an identity for the specified finite local instrument; selective conditioning (dividing one summand by its nonzero trace) is not covered.

derivations.claim: [Coefficient matrix and norm] By [A1], $\Psi=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}e_+\otimes e_--\frac{1}{\sqrt2}e_-\otimes e_+$ is the expansion with $c_{+-}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, $c_{-+}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ and the other coefficients $0$, so the coefficient map $C:W\to V$ is the matrix $C=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ in the bases $(e_+,e_-)$ (columns indexed by $W$), and $\|\Psi\|^2=|c_{+-}|^2+|c_{-+}|^2=1$.

[Partial traces] Computing $CC^*=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=\frac12 I_V$ and $C^*C=\frac12 I_W$, [A2] gives $\operatorname{Tr}_WT_{\Psi,\Psi}=CC^*=\frac12 I_V$ and, by symmetry, $\operatorname{Tr}_VT_{\Psi,\Psi}=C^*C=\frac12 I_W$; both are positive with trace $1$, as they must be for the reduction of a unit vector.

[Purity and Schmidt coefficients] The matrix $\frac12 I_V$ has the single eigenvalue $\frac12$ with multiplicity $2$ (in any basis its matrix is diagonal with entries $\frac12$), so $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2=2\cdot(\frac12)^2=\frac12$ for $\rho=\operatorname{Tr}_WT_{\Psi,\Psi}$; the positive singular values of $C$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of $C^*C=\frac12 I_W$, namely $s_1=s_2=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, so the Schmidt decomposition of $\Psi$ has $k=2$ terms and $\sum_rs_r^2=1$, in agreement with the norm formula of [A2]; since $k=2>1$, $\Psi$ is not a product vector. Finally $T_{\Psi,\Psi}^2=T_{\Psi,\Psi}$ because $T_{\Psi,\Psi}T_{\Psi,\Psi}=\langle\Psi,\Psi\rangle T_{\Psi,\Psi}$ by [A4] and $\|\Psi\|=1$, so $\operatorname{tr}(T_{\Psi,\Psi}^2)=\operatorname{tr}(T_{\Psi,\Psi})=\langle\Psi,\Psi\rangle=1$ by [A3].
